a2010.title: regular customer at a snack bar in Carama II, Bujumbura
a2010.speech: Testifies that this shortage began to show at the end of July: “Today I make do with the 50 cl Amstel.”

a2010.speaker: G.T., customer at a bar in Ngagara III
a2010.name: G.T.
a2010.title: customer at a bar in Ngagara III
a2010.speech: “To get a 65 cl Amstel in a bar in the capital, you have to be a loyal customer” ; “Some traders hide the product in order to sell it at a very high price” ; “Why does Brarudi deprive us of this product when it is available in the interior of the country?”, pointing to Brarudi’s plan to harmonise its bottles with those in circulation in the East African Community.

a2010.speaker: M.A., trader in Brarudi products
a2010.name: M.A.
a2010.title: trader in Brarudi products
a2010.speech: Confides that his supplier sells a crate of Amstel at 26,000 Burundian francs whereas the official price is 19,600 francs, which forces him to sell a 65 cl bottle at between 2,500 and 3,000 francs depending on his relationship with the customer; he also reveals that he does not serve everyone ; “This shortage is made worse by certain traders who export this product to the DRC, where it is much in demand.” He urges Brarudi to take precautions so that these repeated shortages no longer occur.

a2010.speaker: T.S., wholesaler of Brarudi products in the Ngagara zone
a2010.name: T.S.
a2010.title: wholesaler of Brarudi products in the Ngagara zone
a2010.speech: Confides that it has been two weeks since he was last supplied with this product: “It is not available at Brarudi.” Some of his customers have cancelled their orders for lack of the product; he is recording a loss of two million per week.

a2010.speaker: Brarudi (press release of 1 August)
a2010.name: Brarudi (press release of 1 August)
a2010.speech: States that the drinks are available in one format or another, and notes a marked rise in the consumption of its products, explained by three major reasons: the poor banana harvest due to the “Banana bunchy top” virus, which caused a shortage of traditional beer and a shift to industrial beers; the return of customers to bars; and the intense resumption of festive ceremonies. This revival generates increased use of packaging and consequently breakages of bottles and crates, which cannot be replaced optimally because of the country’s shortage of foreign currency. Brarudi has set up a programme to inject 50 cl Amstel packaging ; “The price chain, from Brarudi to the consumer, via the distributors, remains unchanged” ; there have been no major changes in the export of Brarudi drinks.

a2010.speaker: Noel Nkurunziza, president of the Burundian Consumers’ Association (Abuco)
a2010.name: Noel Nkurunziza
a2010.title: president of the Burundian Consumers’ Association (Abuco)
a2010.speech: “Consumers have no information on the current situation. Yet their rights must be respected. They should enjoy the right to information.” ; the reasons put forward by Brarudi only fuel speculation, sometimes about the product that is missing, sometimes about the price that is rising: “So it is the consumers who pay the additional costs.” ; he advises Brarudi to break its silence so that consumers can organise themselves in full knowledge of the facts: “Brarudi does not produce for itself, but rather for the consumers of its products”, and recommends that the administration enforce the official prices.

a2232.speaker: Salma Hamisi, mother of two from Mbagala in Temeke district
a2232.name: Salma Hamisi
a2232.title: mother of two from Mbagala in Temeke district
a2232.speech: "Last year the prices were completely different, we bought children's dresses for Sh25,000 but now it is Sh30,000 and above. Shoes have also gone up, but I cannot let my children miss the joy of Eid."

a2232.speaker: Jamila Said, shopper on Narung'ombe Street
a2232.name: Jamila Said
a2232.title: shopper on Narung'ombe Street
a2232.speech: "This is the children's time; we parents can wear last year's clothes."

a2232.speaker: Mohamed Rashid, father of two buying a kanzu on Nyamwezi Street
a2232.name: Mohamed Rashid
a2232.title: father of two buying a kanzu on Nyamwezi Street
a2232.speech: "This congestion happens every year, but we have no choice. We know we will suffer and be trampled on, but when we get home and the children wear new clothes and play happily, we forget all the hardship."

a2232.speaker: Athumani Salehe, street vendor on Raha Street
a2232.name: Athumani Salehe
a2232.title: street vendor on Raha Street
a2232.speech: Advertised his goods: "Come on, let's go, let's wear abaya and vijora without forgetting your child's clothes at Sh6,000; let's go, mama, love your child so that he can boast to his friends in the neighbourhood."

a2232.speaker: Amina Sheria, trader in madera garments
a2232.name: Amina Sheria
a2232.title: trader in madera garments
a2232.speech: "You find that four of them have come together, you welcome them, they choose, then one of them says that one is bad, let's go; these people spoil our business instead of letting a person decide - they make it their job to run down whatever their companion liked."

a2232.speaker: Peter Selem, vendor of men's clothing
a2232.name: Peter Selem
a2232.title: vendor of men's clothing
a2232.speech: Said that for his part business is not good: "Few people come to the shop; the customers I get are the same ones who come to take wholesale loads and those coming from outside Tanzania, contrary to my expectations - I thought I would gain new customers during this period."

a2232.speaker: Hadija Seif, resident of Upanga
a2232.name: Hadija Seif
a2232.title: resident of Upanga
a2232.speech: "I have come to buy spices at Kariakoo because they are good and not ones that have sat in the shop a long time; the price is cheaper than at other markets, that is why I am here enduring the queue so that I get what is best."

a2453.speaker: International Organization for Migration (IOM)
a2453.name: International Organization for Migration (IOM)
a2453.speech: Announced that between 30 and 31 January 2025 nearly 3,700 households were displaced following fighting in the locality of El Fasher, in North Darfur, bringing to more than 605,000 the total number of displaced people in that region since April 2024 ; also reported a sharp increase in attacks and displacement in other localities of North Darfur since October 2024, notably in Kutum, Kebkabiya, Melit and Al Koma, and that intercommunal conflicts in Dar As Salam contributed nearly 10% of the incidents reported in the region since April 2024.

a2453.speaker: International Organization for Migration (IOM)
a2453.name: International Organization for Migration (IOM)
a2453.speech: Calls on the international community to step up its efforts to provide urgent humanitarian aid and to support efforts aimed at ending this devastating conflict.

a2453.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a2453.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a2453.speech: Expressed major concerns about severe malnutrition, notably in Khartoum State, where more than 70 deaths, mainly among children, have been linked to hunger; the famine conditions at the Abu Shouk displacement camp near El Fasher at the end of December 2024 particularly alarmed OCHA.

a2453.speaker: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR)
a2453.name: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR)
a2453.speech: Highlights growing protection concerns, including the increase in gender-based violence and the heightened risks for children ; also noted that the transit centres in South Sudan are saturated at more than 340% of their capacity, and that in January 2025 more than one million people, including Sudanese refugees and South Sudanese returnees, crossed the border into South Sudan.

a2493.speaker: US government
a2493.name: US government
a2493.speech: Says PEPFAR has provided life-saving antiretroviral treatment and healthcare support to more than 25 million people worldwide since it was first launched in 2003 under President George W. Bush.

a2493.speaker: Russell Vought, White House Office of Management and Budget Director
a2493.name: Russell Vought
a2493.title: White House Office of Management and Budget Director
a2493.speech: Confirmed after a closed-door meeting on Tuesday with Senate Republicans that the administration would support a substitute amendment that leaves PEPFAR funding intact: "There is a substitute amendment that does not include the PEPFAR rescission, and we're fine with that," adding that the overall size of the spending cuts package would remain about $9 billion.

a2493.speaker: The Hill (American newspaper)
a2493.name: The Hill (American newspaper)
a2493.speech: Reported Vought's confirmation that the administration would support a substitute amendment leaving PEPFAR funding intact, and quoted Senate Majority Leader John Thune on the procedural votes.

a2493.speaker: Public health officials and civil society groups
a2493.name: Public health officials and civil society groups
a2493.speech: Had raised alarm over the proposed cuts, warning that any reduction could further put millions at risk of treatment interruption.

a2493.speaker: UNAIDS (report)
a2493.name: UNAIDS (report)
a2493.speech: Warned that abrupt US aid withdrawals had already destabilised supply chains, forced the closure of some HIV treatment facilities, and left thousands of healthcare workers out of jobs in countries like South Africa; it also warned that analysis suggests four million additional AIDS-related deaths between now and 2029, including 300,000 additional children's deaths, if programmes permanently lose PEPFAR's support.

a2493.speaker: Several Republican senators
a2493.name: Several Republican senators
a2493.speech: Argued that slashing the programme's funding would undermine decades of progress in the global HIV/AIDS fight.

a2493.speaker: John Thune, Senate Majority Leader
a2493.name: John Thune
a2493.title: Senate Majority Leader
a2493.speech: Was quoted as saying he planned to hold two procedural votes on Tuesday to advance the package: "Rescissions have been a part of the process around here for a long time, not only in the annual appropriations process," noting that past presidents from both parties had submitted similar proposals to Congress ; he added that the current package represented only a fraction of the federal budget: "What we're talking about here is one tenth of one per cent of all federal spending. That's one-thousandths of the federal budget that's included in this rescissions package."

a2540.speaker: NJ Ayuk, Executive Chairman of the African Energy Chamber (AEC)
a2540.name: NJ Ayuk
a2540.title: Executive Chairman of the African Energy Chamber (AEC)
a2540.speech: Believes that Trump's energy policy represents an opportunity for Africa to fully exploit its vast hydrocarbon resources. "Africa must seize this potentially brief moment in history and see the Trump administration as a partner rather than an adversary," he says ; According to him, international pressure in favour of green energy has held back the continent's industrialisation and economic growth, which remain heavily dependent on fossil fuels. "For too long, these pressures have pushed African countries to abandon their fossil fuel resources in favour of an energy transition that does not always match their immediate needs," he adds ; Ayuk thus encourages African governments to support any promising oil and gas exploration and production project, by simplifying regulations and attracting foreign investment ; As Ayuk stresses: "The next four years under Trump could redefine Africa's energy landscape. The question is whether our leaders will have the courage and foresight needed to take advantage of it."

a2540.speaker: African Energy Chamber (AEC)
a2540.name: African Energy Chamber (AEC)
a2540.speech: The AEC insists that the African reality is different: the continent accounts for only a fraction of global emissions, yet suffers disproportionately from energy poverty.

a2717.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a2717.name: Marco Rubio
a2717.title: US Secretary of State
a2717.speech: decided to boycott the summit after President Donald Trump signed an executive order withdrawing foreign aid, claiming that South Africa was expropriating land from white farmers without compensation under the new Expropriation Act; he was also against the theme of the summit - solidarity, equality and sustainability - claiming that the country was not promoting equality because of the alleged land grabs.

a2717.speaker: Xolisa Mabhongo, South Africa's G20 sous sherpa
a2717.name: Xolisa Mabhongo
a2717.title: South Africa's G20 sous sherpa
a2717.speech: said the US would be represented by a senior diplomat, Dana Brown, at the summit; said all G20 countries are represented; said the G20 operates based on a troika consisting of South Africa, previous host Brazil and the US, and that part of those discussions include the road map towards the US presidency next year. "So, we do not foresee any problems in that." ; "Only one country, the US, will be represented by a senior diplomat."

a2717.speaker: Xolisa Mabhongo, South Africa's G20 sous sherpa
a2717.name: Xolisa Mabhongo
a2717.title: South Africa's G20 sous sherpa
a2717.speech: Responding to the City Press question about Rubio's disapproval of the theme, said the theme was approved by former US president Joe Biden's administration, whose term ended last month, and that the new Trump administration had raised issues because of false information.

a2717.speaker: Xolisa Mabhongo, South Africa's G20 sous sherpa
a2717.name: Xolisa Mabhongo
a2717.title: South Africa's G20 sous sherpa
a2717.speech: said foreign ministers from 15 countries will attend, while four deputy ministers of foreign affairs will represent their nations; said President Cyril Ramaphosa invited 15 other countries as guests to this year's summit, including Spain, the Netherlands, Algeria, Egypt, Angola, the United Arab Emirates and Nigeria.

a2717.speaker: Xolisa Mabhongo, South Africa's G20 sous sherpa
a2717.name: Xolisa Mabhongo
a2717.title: South Africa's G20 sous sherpa
a2717.speech: said there has been an ongoing discussion between South Africa and the US with the hope to resolve the impasse. "This is the beginning of our presidency for the whole year - until the end of November. So, we are in conversations with the US." He emphasised the importance of South Africa's role in the G20, adding that holding the presidency is significant for the country because it allows South Africa to present a development agenda on the G20.

a2717.speaker: Advocate Nokukhanya Jele, South Africa's G20 sous sherpa
a2717.name: Advocate Nokukhanya Jele
a2717.title: South Africa's G20 sous sherpa
a2717.speech: said the G20 carries tremendous responsibility because the decisions taken by the summit directly impact the lives of the global community. "The world faces a myriad of global challenges and continues to suffer developmental reversals. The current global situation suggests that the international community requires a profound paradigm shift characterised by solidarity, harmony, and mutual respect. In this regard, the G20 has a significant role to play in fostering global cooperation and collaboration to address the challenges and achieve sustainable development."

a2719.speaker: Fuse ODG, British-Ghanaian singer
a2719.name: Fuse ODG
a2719.title: British-Ghanaian singer
a2719.speech: said his latest track is "not just a song" but "a statement"; declared live on ITV's Good Morning Britain programme that "African problems need to be solved by Africans".

a2719.speaker: Ed Sheeran, singer
a2719.name: Ed Sheeran
a2719.title: singer
a2719.speech: said last month that Band Aid had not asked for permission to re-use his vocals from a 30th anniversary version of their track, and credited Fuse ODG for updating his view of the situation: "A decade on and my understanding of the narrative associated with this has changed, eloquently explained by @fuseodg".

a2719.speaker: Fuse ODG, British-Ghanaian singer (social media post)
a2719.name: Fuse ODG
a2719.title: British-Ghanaian singer (social media post)
a2719.speech: "I refused to participate in Band Aid because I recognised the harm initiatives like it inflict on Africa. While they may generate sympathy and donations, they perpetuate damaging stereotypes that stifle Africa's economic growth, tourism, and investment, ultimately costing the continent trillions and destroying its dignity, pride and identity."

a2719.speaker: Fuse ODG, British-Ghanaian singer
a2719.name: Fuse ODG
a2719.title: British-Ghanaian singer
a2719.speech: Speaking about We Know It's Christmas (Band Aid Reply), said it was intended as "a reflection of where we've come from and where we're going". "Ten years ago, I made a stand because I believed it was time for Africans to tell their own stories and to redefine the narrative." ; "This song is a celebration of that shift. We're no longer waiting for charity; we're building our own futures." ; "This is about empowerment, pride, and showing the world that Africa's story is far more than poverty and aid."

a2719.speaker: Tony Hadley, Spandau Ballet singer
a2719.name: Tony Hadley
a2719.title: Spandau Ballet singer
a2719.speech: told BBC Radio 2 that critics like Sheeran "should shut up, to be honest." "If you take that route, then nobody does anything to help anybody. So it's just nonsense... Everybody's doing their bit to try and support various charities and we were doing our bit, innocently, to support what was happening in Ethiopia... So what do we do? Do we sit back and do nothing?"

a2719.speaker: Fuse ODG, British-Ghanaian singer
a2719.name: Fuse ODG
a2719.title: British-Ghanaian singer
a2719.speech: Speaking to BBC Breakfast last month, commented that while the original Band Aid project had been "touching" and well-intentioned, the lyrics and connected images were now having a damaging effect and stopping people from visiting Africa. "It's been touching seeing the efforts that were put into it initially, the British public and different celebrities coming together to support a good cause, because there was a crisis at the time they needed attending to." ; "I have no problem with that, I think that was fantastic, and even just watching it back, I'm even getting emotional." ; "But in that act of kindness, in that process of trying to help a crisis, we created another identity crisis." ; "As a child who's now grown up in this era of images like that, Band Aid and initiatives like it have put Africa as a place of famine, a place of poverty, disease-filled. It took away our collective sense of pride and identity. So in the middle of trying to solve a temporary crisis, we've caused another dangerous crisis, which is an identity crisis for a whole continent."

a2719.speaker: Fuse ODG, British-Ghanaian singer
a2719.name: Fuse ODG
a2719.title: British-Ghanaian singer
a2719.speech: told BBC Africa that despite having been "excited" initially to be invited to take part in the latest rendition of the star-studded charity track, his over-arching "mission" as an artist was to "realign how the world sees Africa and how Africans feel about themselves". "It hit me that the images that the Band Aid project portrays just did not align with our mission to portray Africa in a positive light." ; "There's also starving children in the UK."

a2719.speaker: Midge Ure, Band Aid co-writer
a2719.name: Midge Ure
a2719.title: Band Aid co-writer
a2719.speech: recently acknowledged the criticisms of Band Aid's approach in the modern climate, saying it was "unfortunate" that Sheeran had not been contacted about the 2024 mix. "I understand the whole thing about the 'white saviour complex'," he told Radio 2's Jeremy Vine. "It's not new. We've had this thrown at us for 40 years." However, he said the song was not about portraying Africa in a negative light, but was trying to show the real-life consequences "of famine, of war, of conflict". "And the result is children who need food, who need medication, who need education, and that's what we deal with."

a2725.speaker: Michael James Macchio, Director of Abyssinia Luxury Coach
a2725.name: Michael James Macchio
a2725.title: Director of Abyssinia Luxury Coach
a2725.speech: Confirmed to local media that the first cross-border bus transportation service has been launched between Nairobi and Addis Ababa ; said the launch introduces a direct bus connection between the two capital cities, filling a service gap left by previous operators.

a2725.speaker: Ethiopian Ministry of Transport and Logistics (statement)
a2725.name: Ethiopian Ministry of Transport and Logistics (statement)
a2725.speech: Disclosed on Thursday that it was not aware of the launch of bus public transport between Nairobi and Addis Ababa ; citing the launch of the ground transportation by Abyssinia Luxury Coach, the ministry said it was done without its knowledge.

a2725.speaker: Ethiopian Ministry of Transport and Logistics
a2725.name: Ethiopian Ministry of Transport and Logistics
a2725.speech: Announced that while there was a national plan to start the service next Ethiopian fiscal year (2025/2026) to create a connection between the two countries, the process requires a cooperation agreement, joint tariff setting, and other diplomatic issues between the two countries.

a3245.speaker: Seed Co
a3245.name: Seed Co
a3245.speech: Says it is linking horticulture producers with local and export markets as it expands activities in that sector.

a3245.speaker: Felistus Ndawi, Seed Co general manager for the vegetables unit
a3245.name: Felistus Ndawi
a3245.title: Seed Co general manager for the vegetables unit
a3245.speech: Told The Financial Gazette that horticulture, unlike the production of field crops such as maize and wheat, required more market support: "When it comes to..."

a3413.speaker: Armed Forces of Liberia and the US Government (press release)
a3413.name: Armed Forces of Liberia and the US Government (press release)
a3413.speech: According to a release issued recently, the new Tuberculosis Clinic at the 14th Military Hospital in Duazon, Margibi County, reaffirms the US Government's longstanding commitment to support Liberia's public health infrastructure; the release added that the Tuberculosis Clinic will also be used to assist Liberians throughout the country as a central treatment center.

a3790.speaker: Report distributed by the APO Group on behalf of the United Nations Secretary-General
a3790.name: Report distributed by the APO Group on behalf of the United Nations Secretary-General
a3790.speech: Stated that her experience also includes working on agricultural and rural development policies in Africa, Asia and Latin America ; added that she holds a master's degree in management of public policies from Sciences Po Paris, a postgraduate in agricultural economics at the University of London and Agroindustries in Montpellier.

a4106.speaker: Maxime Rabilloud, General Manager of TotalEnergies
a4106.name: Maxime Rabilloud
a4106.title: General Manager of TotalEnergies
a4106.speech: stated: “we are here to express our solidarity with the families affected by Cyclone Chido on behalf of all Mozambique LNG Project partners and in reaction to the Government’s call to support the affected communities.”

a4106.speaker: Valige Tauabo, Governor of Cabo Delgado
a4106.name: Valige Tauabo
a4106.title: Governor of Cabo Delgado
a4106.speech: recognized TotalEnergies efforts for its ongoing commitment to disaster relief and humanitarian assistance ; “We recognize that this support alone will not solve all the challenges caused by Cyclone Chido. That is why we continue to mobilize additional resources. In the meantime, we encourage the population to rebuild their homes and strengthen agricultural production to ensure food security and income generation”

a4472.speaker: Fenella Frost, UNDP Malawi Resident Representative
a4472.name: Fenella Frost
a4472.title: UNDP Malawi Resident Representative
a4472.speech: Confirmed that UNDP Malawi, in collaboration with other development partners, has committed $8.3 million (approximately K14.5 billion) for the September 16 General Elections, and said the Malawi Electoral Support Project (MESP) Basket Fund initiative, running from 2023 to 2025, is designed to bolster the country’s electoral processes, ensuring free, fair and credible elections: “The partners include the European Union (EU), the United States Agency for International Development (USaid), the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), the Royal Norwegian Embassy and the Embassy of Ireland.”

a4472.speaker: Rune Skinnebach, European Union Ambassador to Malawi
a4472.name: Rune Skinnebach
a4472.title: European Union Ambassador to Malawi
a4472.speech: Said the EU and partners reaffirmed their commitment to supporting Malawi’s electoral process through their contribution to the election basket fund, and that, as in previous elections, the bloc remains the largest donor to the basket fund: “The EU is the biggest donor in the basket fund, which is doing a number of activities to support the elections. However, the elections are primarily funded by the government, and the Malawi Electoral Commission has been assured that, once again, appropriate government funding will be made available, ensuring the smooth organisation of the polls.”

a4472.speaker: Rune Skinnebach, European Union Ambassador to Malawi
a4472.name: Rune Skinnebach
a4472.title: European Union Ambassador to Malawi
a4472.speech: On EU election observation: “I expect the mission will confirm the feasibility, and then we will deploy a large EU election monitoring team a few months before the elections to assess and document the electoral process.”

a4804.speaker: A new report (regional HIV prevalence report presented at the Regional Health Assembly)
a4804.name: A new report (regional HIV prevalence report presented at the Regional Health Assembly)
a4804.speech: Reveals that new cases of HIV/Aids in the Acholi region had lowered by 72 percent from 11,358 in 2017 to just 3,175 in 2021. The report indicates that HIV cases are higher among females at 9.3 percent compared to 5.3 percent among males in the region, and that only 84 percent of viral load suppression had been achieved for all ages but was much lower among children under 14 years old.

a4804.speaker: Peter Erem, Director of Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning at The Aids Support Organization (TASO)
a4804.name: Peter Erem
a4804.title: Director of Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning at The Aids Support Organization (TASO)
a4804.speech: Presenting the regional HIV prevalence report, says new cases of HIV being diagnosed had reduced significantly in the last four years. He also noted that the region has registered a reduction in the prevalence at 7.4 percent in 2021, a 15 percent [drop] from 8.7 percent in 2017, and that the National HIV prevalence stood at 5.3 percent by 2021. According to Erem, whereas the region has achieved the 95 percent targets of HIV patients being on ART treatment and knowing their status, the challenge remains on viral load suppression among adults and children.

a4804.speaker: Dr. Peter Mukobi, Director of Gulu Regional Referral Hospital
a4804.name: Dr. Peter Mukobi
a4804.title: Director of Gulu Regional Referral Hospital
a4804.speech: Says the project will be helpful for the community in improving access to services. He says the project seeks to improve services in the areas of maternal, and neonatal child health, HIV, TB, and Nutrition, citing that it will be a big boost for the facility.

a4804.speaker: Dr. Abel Nkolo, Chief of Party, USAID RHITES-N in Acholi
a4804.name: Dr. Abel Nkolo
a4804.title: Chief of Party, USAID RHITES-N in Acholi
a4804.speech: Noted that they are grateful for their continued partnerships with the district authorities in addressing health concerns in the region. “We hope to continue to work together to improve overall health in Acholi Sub-region.”

a4804.speaker: Chris Mugarura, Assistant Commissioner in charge of the Health Policy and Sector Planning Division, Health Ministry
a4804.name: Chris Mugarura
a4804.title: Assistant Commissioner in charge of the Health Policy and Sector Planning Division, Health Ministry
a4804.speech: Lauded the planners of the health assembly saying it’s an avenue to enlist the help of decision-makers and funders in order to improve access to healthcare.

a4804.speaker: Chris Mugarura, Assistant Commissioner in charge of the Health Policy and Sector Planning Division, Health Ministry
a4804.name: Chris Mugarura
a4804.title: Assistant Commissioner in charge of the Health Policy and Sector Planning Division, Health Ministry
a4804.speech: Says whereas the country has made great strides in bringing services nearer to the people, the quality still remains low, arguing that there is a need to shift focus on sharing knowledge on evidence-based strategies.

a5020.speaker: John Mahama, former President of Ghana
a5020.name: John Mahama
a5020.title: former President of Ghana
a5020.speech: Stated: “The Western Region is one of the most important regions in this country because of its enormous contribution to the advancement of Ghana.”

a5020.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, former President of Ghana
a5020.name: John Dramani Mahama
a5020.title: former President of Ghana
a5020.speech: Has promised to restore our founder and first president of Ghana his rightful place in our country’s history.

a5020.speaker: Akufo-Addo-Bawumia-led New Patriotic Party (NPP) government
a5020.name: Akufo-Addo-Bawumia-led New Patriotic Party (NPP) government
a5020.speech: Made grand declarations about transforming our region into an oil services hub with world-class port facilities ; pledged to construct a new regional hospital, rehabilitate the Effia-Nkwanta Hospital, and modernize the Takoradi Port ; spoke of establishing an Accident and Emergency Centre in Takoradi and an oil refinery in Sekondi-Takoradi.

a5103.speaker: Ethiopia (government)
a5103.name: Ethiopia (government)
a5103.speech: In May, described the US ambassador's intervention in its internal affairs as “unsolicited advice.”

a5103.speaker: Gallup (poll on the perception of global leadership)
a5103.name: Gallup (poll on the perception of global leadership)
a5103.speech: According to the poll, the median approval rating of the United States in Africa fell from 59% in 2022 to 56% in 2023; among the world's major powers, the United States is the only one whose image in Africa did not improve this year.

a5103.speaker: US Census Bureau
a5103.name: US Census Bureau
a5103.speech: According to the Bureau, US-Africa trade fell from 113 billion dollars in 2010 to 67.4 billion in 2023.

a5103.speaker: Cameron Hudson, Senior Fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS)
a5103.name: Cameron Hudson
a5103.title: Senior Fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS)
a5103.speech: Stresses that this lack of results, combined with excessive promises, has only reinforced Washington's image as an unreliable and hypocritical partner.

a5103.speaker: William Ruto, President of Kenya
a5103.name: William Ruto
a5103.title: President of Kenya
a5103.speech: Was indignant at the treatment of African leaders at the 2022 US-Africa summit, declaring that it was inappropriate to “cram us into buses like schoolchildren.”

a5103.speaker: Arikana Chihombori-Quao, former African Union representative to the United States
a5103.name: Arikana Chihombori-Quao
a5103.title: former African Union representative to the United States
a5103.speech: Added that this lack of respect illustrates the historical attitude of the United States towards Africa.

a5103.speaker: Seco Cassama, Bissau-Guinean political scientist
a5103.name: Seco Cassama
a5103.title: Bissau-Guinean political scientist
a5103.speech: Believes that the United States imposes its interests without taking African traditions and civilizations into account. He cites the example of the American military presence in Niger, where, despite the opening of Air Base 201 in Agadez in 2018, terrorist attacks have continued to increase, underlining the ineffectiveness of American strategies.

a5103.speaker: Fred M'membe, president of the Socialist Party of Zambia
a5103.name: Fred M'membe
a5103.title: president of the Socialist Party of Zambia
a5103.speech: During Vice President Kamala Harris's visit in March 2023, criticized the United States for its historical interference in Africa while today setting itself up as a promoter of democracy.

a5103.speaker: The Herald (Zimbabwean newspaper)
a5103.name: The Herald (Zimbabwean newspaper)
a5103.speech: According to the newspaper, this American attitude, combined with its economic power, is perceived as a form of arrogance that fuels resentment in Africa.

a5125.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi
a5125.name: Lazarus Chakwera
a5125.title: President of Malawi
a5125.speech: Appeared on the State broadcaster a week before the September 16 General Election, accusing some bureaucrats of sabotaging the country's fuel supply and promised to take action after the poll ; “We will be back soon!”

a5125.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi
a5125.name: Lazarus Chakwera
a5125.title: President of Malawi
a5125.speech: Was back on air last Wednesday, conceding defeat to Democratic Progressive Party's torchbearer Peter Mutharika, who won 57 percent of the vote.

a5125.speaker: Constitutional Court of Malawi (2020 judgement)
a5125.name: Constitutional Court of Malawi (2020 judgement)
a5125.speech: Annulled Mutharika's re-election in 2019 and ordered a fresh presidential election.

a5125.speaker: UK Government inquiry into Sattar's money laundering cases
a5125.name: UK Government inquiry into Sattar's money laundering cases
a5125.speech: Implicated several high-level officials in Malawi, exposing the vulnerability of elected officials and the conflict of interest that would arise.

a5263.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi (State of the Nation Address)
a5263.name: Lazarus Chakwera
a5263.title: President of Malawi (State of the Nation Address)
a5263.speech: Highlighted some of the progress made "that has come from the painful surgery on Malawi after four years of endurance; the pain that Malawians have gone through because of this surgical shift from personal interest to national development." "I stand before you, Madam Speaker, to report the Food Security Development, the Economic Development, the Governance Development, the Human Capital Development, and the Infrastructure Development I have delivered in each district as a result of the patience and endurance of Malawians who allowed me to serve them. In fact, Madam Speaker, I stand before you to present a good report of good developments that I believe the good people of Malawi will want us to take forward. For this reason, Madam Speaker, the title of my address today is: 'Taking Our Development Forward to Continue the Progress We Have Delivered'."

a5263.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi (State of the Nation Address)
a5263.name: Lazarus Chakwera
a5263.title: President of Malawi (State of the Nation Address)
a5263.speech: Reported, district by district, on the food security development his Administration has delivered over the past four years, including irrigation investment through the Programme for Rural Irrigation Development (PRIDE), support to farmers under the Affordable Inputs Programme (AIP) with a "steady graduation from the programme", fertilizer loans through the National Economic Empowerment Fund (NEEF), support to Mega Farmers through the MEGA Farm Unit, maize distribution to food-insecure households, and school feeding programmes in primary schools across the districts.

a5263.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi (State of the Nation Address)
a5263.name: Lazarus Chakwera
a5263.title: President of Malawi (State of the Nation Address)
a5263.speech: Reported on economic development delivered in each district, including communication towers and Last Mile Connectivity, electrification of trading centres and households through MAREP 9 and MEAP, home-solar installations, free water connections, NEEF and MAIIC loans to people starting business ventures, AGCOM support to cooperatives, social cash transfers and incomes provided under the Climate Smart Enhanced Public Works.

a5263.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi (State of the Nation Address)
a5263.name: Lazarus Chakwera
a5263.title: President of Malawi (State of the Nation Address)
a5263.speech: Reported on governance development, including the establishment of District Land Tribunals, recruitment of District Land Registrars, devolution of land functions, and work with magistrate courts to increase people's understanding of how to interpret and implement gender laws; and on human capital development, including the construction of community day secondary schools, primary and secondary school blocks, teachers' houses built with the Constituency Development Fund, the recruitment of primary and secondary school teachers to reduce the teacher-pupil ratio, and the construction and rehabilitation of health posts.

a5263.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi (State of the Nation Address)
a5263.name: Lazarus Chakwera
a5263.title: President of Malawi (State of the Nation Address)
a5263.speech: Reported on infrastructure development, including the Meru Garrison housing units, the Chitipa-Ilomba Road and the 260km Rumphi-Nyika-Chitipa Road, the US$26.7-million Karonga Town Water Supply Project "now nearly done at 98%" thanks to OFID and BADEA, the upgrade of Karonga airport runway, the Commercial Court in Blantyre at 98% progress, the rehabilitation of the Chileka terminal building at 95% completion, the National Aquatic Complex and Griffin Saenda Indoor Sports Complex, the planned Twin Towers at Capital Hill, the Millennium Challenge Account (MCA) Compact funded 53km Chileka-Malingunde-Likuni Road, a planned new international airport in Lilongwe, the Judicial Complex Project signed with the People's Republic of China, and the Malawi Water Supply and Sanitation Project (2022-2028).

a5263.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi (State of the Nation Address)
a5263.name: Lazarus Chakwera
a5263.title: President of Malawi (State of the Nation Address)
a5263.speech: Said of his vision for the districts that he plans to see Chitipa "become a major corridor for trade between Malawi, Tanzania, and Zambia", Karonga "truly becoming the bread basket of Malawi" and "a mining powerhouse that finances its development", and told voters in each district: "Be ready to hear other parties this year offering to take [the district] backward, but remember that the reason I am here is to continue taking your development forward."

a5263.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi (State of the Nation Address)
a5263.name: Lazarus Chakwera
a5263.title: President of Malawi (State of the Nation Address)
a5263.speech: "Madam Speaker, I have taken long deliberately because this is a House of records and I want it to be on record that this is what I have delivered for the Malawian people in the four years that I have been President." ; "And I believe that I am at peace with God and I have enough trust in the Malawian people that they are fair-minded enough to judge my performance as President by what I have done, not by what other politicians say about me or by the disasters that have befallen us as a nation and subjected us to a season of pain that we must have the strength to endure and overcome, and I believe that overcome we will."

a5313.speaker: Fabian Michael Lai, Acting CEO of the National Oil Company of Liberia (NOCAL)
a5313.name: Fabian Michael Lai
a5313.title: Acting CEO of the National Oil Company of Liberia (NOCAL)
a5313.speech: Delivered a comprehensive progress report on NOCAL's partnership with TGS NOPEC, saying the strategic partnership has resulted in the acquisition of an extensive multi-client 2D and 3D seismic survey program covering over 15,000 square kilometers of Liberia's offshore basins, which has positioned Liberia as a promising player in the energy sector, attracting interest and investment from super-majors and independent oil companies; he emphasized the partnership's economic impact, stating that Liberia currently receives 80% of revenues from legacy 3D data sales.

a5313.speaker: President Joseph Nyuma Boakai of Liberia
a5313.name: President Joseph Nyuma Boakai of Liberia
a5313.speech: Lauded TGS NOPEC for its enduring partnership and highlighted its significant role in the country's frontier oil and gas industry and national development; underscoring the difficult circumstances faced by the country, particularly regarding the reduction in USAID aid, he proffered the need for increased CSR contributions in order to solidify TGS NOPEC as a responsible partner, and further mandated a follow-up with TGS NOPEC on increasing its CSR contributions, while also exploring additional avenues for collaboration.

a5313.speaker: Fabian Michael Lai, Acting CEO of NOCAL
a5313.name: Fabian Michael Lai
a5313.title: Acting CEO of NOCAL
a5313.speech: Indicated that the partnership is not just about data and profits, but also about empowering the people and building a future where Liberians lead their energy sector; revealed annual contributions of US$200,000 for social and welfare programs, including the renovation of the Intensive Care Unit and expansion of the trauma unit at the John F. Kennedy Medical Center with a total investment of US$15,000, medical equipment valued at US$60,000 and ICU beds costing US$142,955; and highlighted the support for market women and the Group of 77 by providing US$40,000 towards initiatives that benefit women entrepreneurs and the disabled.

a5313.speaker: Fabian Michael Lai, Acting CEO of NOCAL
a5313.name: Fabian Michael Lai
a5313.title: Acting CEO of NOCAL
a5313.speech: Shared his leadership's plans to attract additional investment with the anticipated executive allocation and conduct further geological and geophysical studies onshore, and said plans are underway to conduct a feasibility study on constructing a shore base to support offshore exploration activities, which will create jobs and stimulate local economies; he reaffirmed his team's unwavering commitment to leveraging the partnership with TGS NOPEC for the collective benefit of all Liberians and emphasized their determination to ensure that the energy sector transforms into a cornerstone of national development.

a5375.speaker: Professor Ali Muhammad Pate, Nigeria's Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a5375.name: Professor Ali Muhammad Pate
a5375.title: Nigeria's Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a5375.speech: Has declared that building a sustainable health system requires deliberate investment by Nigerians themselves, warning that the illusion of depending solely on external aid to finance healthcare is "foolish" ; "Health, wherever it is found, is not cheap. If you want to get good health, you have to pay for it. Somebody has to pay for it. The illusion that you can get quality health without investing is foolish."

a5375.speaker: Professor Ali Muhammad Pate, Nigeria's Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a5375.name: Professor Ali Muhammad Pate
a5375.title: Nigeria's Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a5375.speech: "This is the context of the health reforms that Nigeria is undertaking under this president." ; "When the president decided to prioritize health as a key pillar of his Renewed Hope agenda, we laid out a mission to save lives, reduce physical and financial pain, produce health, and to do it for all Nigerians. That is our translation of universal health coverage."

a5375.speaker: Professor Ali Muhammad Pate, Nigeria's Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a5375.name: Professor Ali Muhammad Pate
a5375.title: Nigeria's Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a5375.speech: According to him, Nigeria currently spends an average of just $120 per person annually on health, with two-thirds of that amount coming directly from households; less than $30 per person is contributed by all tiers of government, while development partners account for under 10 percent of the total spend. "It is like a bicycle compared to the Rolls Royce of other economies that invest massively in health."

a5375.speaker: Professor Ali Muhammad Pate, Nigeria's Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a5375.name: Professor Ali Muhammad Pate
a5375.title: Nigeria's Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a5375.speech: Outlined the four pillars of the Tinubu administration's reforms: strengthening governance and accountability; expanding population health outcomes through primary care and health insurance; unlocking the health value chain to produce essential commodities locally; and building resilience through stronger health security and digital transformation.

a5375.speaker: Dr. Iziaq Adekunle Salako, Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a5375.name: Dr. Iziaq Adekunle Salako
a5375.title: Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a5375.speech: Hinted that Nigeria is on the path of reimagining its health financing structure with renewed commitment from the Federal Government to strengthen domestic resource mobilization and reduce dependence on external aid; described the gathering as a crucial step in reshaping the country's health financing landscape; noted that the dialogue must go beyond discussion to actionable strategies that will inspire outcomes and guide future policies, stressing that President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has given clear directives to prioritize health sector financing as a pillar for national growth.

a5375.speaker: Dr. Iziaq Adekunle Salako, Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a5375.name: Dr. Iziaq Adekunle Salako
a5375.title: Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a5375.speech: Highlighted the government's budgetary strides, revealing that Nigeria's health allocation grew from N434 billion in 2018 to N1.02 trillion in 2021, with a substantial increase to N2.48 trillion in 2025, equivalent to 5.18% of the total federal budget; acknowledged that while this represents progress, it still falls short of the 15% Abuja Declaration benchmark; added that the National Assembly's additional N300 billion allocation in 2024, following the suspension of U.S. aid, further boosted available funds for the sector; commended subnational governments for scaling up their health budgets, with total health expenditure as a share of GDP rising to 5.03% in 2024.

a5375.speaker: Dr. Iziaq Adekunle Salako, Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a5375.name: Dr. Iziaq Adekunle Salako
a5375.title: Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a5375.speech: Reaffirming the Ministry's commitment to Universal Health Coverage, said the government is set to enroll at least 44 million Nigerians into health insurance by 2030 through the National Health Insurance Authority Act of 2022; emphasized that reforms such as increasing the Basic Health Care Provision Fund to 2% of consolidated revenue, reducing out-of-pocket spending, and adopting lessons from successful models in Ghana and Kenya would be critical to achieving sustainable financing; called on stakeholders at the dialogue to contribute innovative ideas and forge strong partnerships to ensure that every Nigerian has access to quality healthcare without financial hardship.

a5375.speaker: Dr. Kelechi Ohiri, Director-General of the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA)
a5375.name: Dr. Kelechi Ohiri
a5375.title: Director-General of the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA)
a5375.speech: Underscored that Nigeria is at a critical juncture amid "multiple transitions" from shifts in global health financing to the rising burden of non-communicable diseases and demographic changes. "We are all witnesses to the changes going on globally with Development Assistance for Health. The world we knew in overseas development assistance is gone. Going forward, it has to be a lot more reliance on domestic resources. Nigeria, at the last World Health Assembly, played a key role in adopting a landmark resolution to strengthen health financing globally. Now, we are bringing that conversation home."

a5375.speaker: Dr. Kelechi Ohiri, Director-General of the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA)
a5375.name: Dr. Kelechi Ohiri
a5375.title: Director-General of the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA)
a5375.speech: Stressed the urgency of reducing high out-of-pocket spending, improving financial protection, and ensuring better coordination across federal, state, and local governments. "Nigeria is people. People must be at the center of the health system, and at the center of what we are financing."

a5458.speaker: Maria Zakharova, Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson
a5458.name: Maria Zakharova
a5458.title: Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson
a5458.speech: Russian-African cooperation is developing and reaching a new level.

a5458.speaker: Zeynalova, Russian Ambassador (to Mauritius)
a5458.name: Zeynalova
a5458.title: Russian Ambassador (to Mauritius)
a5458.speech: Russia and Mauritius intend to increase trade turnover.

a5458.speaker: DR Congo authorities
a5458.name: DR Congo authorities
a5458.speech: Have accused Rwanda of occupying Bukavu.

a5458.speaker: Head of the Ugandan army
a5458.name: Head of the Ugandan army
a5458.speech: Has threatened to attack the town of Bunia in eastern DR Congo.

a5458.speaker: UN Secretary General
a5458.name: UN Secretary General
a5458.speech: Calls for talks amid M23 rebel advance in Bukavu.

a5458.speaker: Ambassador (unnamed)
a5458.name: Ambassador (unnamed)
a5458.speech: Rwanda is not the cause of the conflict in eastern DR Congo.

a5458.speaker: Sudanese army (reported by media)
a5458.name: Sudanese army (reported by media)
a5458.speech: The Sudanese army rejected the UAE's call for a truce during Ramadan.

a5458.speaker: European Parliament
a5458.name: European Parliament
a5458.speech: Called for the freezing of EU aid to Rwanda due to the conflict in the DRC.

a5458.speaker: RFI
a5458.name: RFI
a5458.speech: Zelensky's attempt to get to the AU summit caused protests among the participants.

a5458.speaker: Expert (unnamed)
a5458.name: Expert (unnamed)
a5458.speech: The expert explained how the reorganization of USAID is related to the US strategy in Africa.

a5830.speaker: Antony Blinken, US Secretary of State
a5830.name: Antony Blinken
a5830.title: US Secretary of State
a5830.speech: Has described the attacks on civilians in Gaza as gut-wrenching, saying "the suffering among innocent men, women and children breaks my heart" ; said his government has impressed upon Israel its responsibility to minimise civilian casualties and get in more humanitarian assistance through to Gazans ; "It's why we're at it relentlessly, every single day. Just on a purely human level, it's devastating, but it reinforces the conviction that there has to be another way that answers Israel's most profound concerns and questions." ; "Israelis have to live with security. They can't have a repeat of October 7th. No country would accept a repeat of October 7th. And I think not by way of justification, but just by way of explanation. It's hard to overstate the psychological impact on the country as a whole of what happened on that day."

a5830.speaker: Israel (government position)
a5830.name: Israel (government position)
a5830.speech: Has maintained it has a right to defend itself.

a5830.speaker: World Economic Forum report
a5830.name: World Economic Forum report
a5830.speech: A WEF report released at the start of the WEF annual meeting on Monday found that global growth would likely suffer in 2024 as a result of these geopolitical issues, with Europe already on the backfoot expected to bear the brunt of the worst economic growth levels.

a5830.speaker: Adel Al-Jubeir, Saudi Arabia's Foreign Affairs Minister
a5830.name: Adel Al-Jubeir
a5830.title: Saudi Arabia's Foreign Affairs Minister
a5830.speech: Stated that the security of navigation in the Red Sea was a concern for all countries. He said the priority was de-escalation of hostilities in the Red Sea and the entire region ; "We need to focus on the war in Gaza because of its impact first on the region as a whole and for the risks it poses for further escalation. We've now seen close to 30 000 civilians being killed in Gaza. They are killed every day, and we continue to see restrictions to humanitarian aid and frankly, we don't see any sign that Israel is achieving its strategic objectives."

a5830.speaker: South Africa's top legal minds (before the International Court of Justice)
a5830.name: South Africa's top legal minds (before the International Court of Justice)
a5830.speech: Presented their case to the International Court of Justice, seeking for Israel's attack to cease immediately.

a5841.speaker: Karonga District Council
a5841.name: Karonga District Council
a5841.speech: Has issued an urgent appeal for humanitarian assistance following heavy floods that have displaced over 1,000 households and left three people dead.

a5841.speaker: George Mponda, Karonga District Council Public Relations Officer
a5841.name: George Mponda
a5841.title: Karonga District Council Public Relations Officer
a5841.speech: Described the situation as dire, with floodwaters submerging entire villages after torrential rains pounded the district from March 25 to March 30, 2025. "The situation is critical. We have 1,017 households affected, with 161 families currently seeking shelter in three emergency camps set up in Senior Chief Kilupula's area. Many people have lost their homes and belongings, and they urgently need food, shelter, and other basic supplies." ; "The camps such as Chimalabanthu Village Camp, Chakwera Village Camp, and Yalero Village Camp are accommodating families who have nowhere else to go. Tragically, three lives have been lost, including a man who was struck by lightning and two children who drowned in the Kyungu River. Additionally, two women were injured by lightning and are receiving medical treatment."

a5841.speaker: Area and Village Disaster Risk Management Committees (ADRMCs and VDRMCs) initial assessment
a5841.name: Area and Village Disaster Risk Management Committees (ADRMCs and VDRMCs) initial assessment
a5841.speech: According to an initial assessment conducted by the Committees, the immediate needs of the affected families include food, shelter materials such as tents and tarpaulins, blankets, mosquito nets, sleeping mats, kitchen utensils, and clothing.

a5855.speaker: Moroccan Ministry of Foreign Affairs, African Cooperation and Moroccans Residing Abroad (communique)
a5855.name: Moroccan Ministry of Foreign Affairs
a5855.title: African Cooperation and Moroccans Residing Abroad (communique)
a5855.speech: The Kingdom of Morocco welcomes the progress made towards halting the hostilities and attacks against Palestinian civilians under way since 7 October 2023 ; "the Kingdom calls on all Palestinian and Israeli parties to give peace a chance and to demonstrate sincere and constructive commitment, far from any circumstantial or opportunistic considerations" ; "The Kingdom expresses the wish that this ceasefire agreement be fully respected, and that it allow the halting of attacks against civilians, the return of displaced persons, and the smooth access of humanitarian aid in sufficient quantities." ; "the ceasefire agreement should open the way to a genuine peace process, allowing the establishment of a Palestinian State within the 1967 borders with East Jerusalem as its capital, living side by side and in peace with Israel."

a5855.speaker: King Mohammed VI of Morocco, chair of the Al-Quds Committee
a5855.name: King Mohammed VI of Morocco
a5855.title: chair of the Al-Quds Committee
a5855.speech: Stressed, notably in his message to the last Arab Summit, that "it is essential to avoid emerging from one crisis only to enter another."

a5855.speaker: Agence marocaine de presse (MAP)
a5855.name: Agence marocaine de presse (MAP)
a5855.speech: Reported on Friday that Morocco welcomes the progress made towards halting the hostilities, citing the communique of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, African Cooperation and Moroccans Residing Abroad.

a5932.speaker: Paul Kagame, President of Rwanda
a5932.name: Paul Kagame
a5932.title: President of Rwanda
a5932.speech: "President Trump has an unconventional way of doing things," Kagame said in an interview with CNN reporter Larry Madowo. "I completely agree with him on many things." ; when pressed by a CNN reporter to explain how the shutdown of USAID might negatively affect Rwanda, said that the country might actually benefit from the cessation of USAID funds: "I think from being hurt, we might learn some lessons."

a5932.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5932.name: Donald Trump
a5932.title: US President
a5932.speech: Has repeatedly signaled that the US Agency for International Development (USAID) should be shut down and cease to distribute taxpayer funds around the world to aid and relief projects; previously told reporters on Sunday that USAID is "run by radical lunatics" ; has also signaled that DOGE, which is tasked with eliminating government spending and waste and streamlining operations, will investigate the Education Department and the Pentagon.

a5932.speaker: U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols (court ruling)
a5932.name: U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols (court ruling)
a5932.speech: A Trump appointee, agreed to block an order that would have given just 30 days for the thousands of overseas USAID workers the administration wanted to place on abrupt administrative leave to move their families back to the U.S. at the government's expense.

a5932.speaker: Larry Madowo, CNN reporter (@LarryMadowo, post on X)
a5932.name: Larry Madowo
a5932.title: CNN reporter (@LarryMadowo, post on X)
a5932.speech: "President Paul Kagame says he 'completely agrees with President Trump on many things' after he froze US foreign aid and closed USAID. The Rwandan president tells me that African countries must wean themselves off aid."

a5933.speaker: Donald Trump, US President (executive order “Further Modifying the Reciprocal Tariff Rates”)
a5933.name: Donald Trump
a5933.title: US President (executive order “Further Modifying the Reciprocal Tariff Rates”)
a5933.speech: Issued an executive order titled “Further Modifying the Reciprocal Tariff Rates”, which saw tariffs on goods from several African countries – including Namibia – reduced to 15%; Namibia’s tariff was cut from 21% to 15%, while Angola’s dropped from 32%, Botswana’s from 37%, Zimbabwe’s from 18%, Lesotho’s from 50%, and Zambia’s from 17%, with South Africa excluded and its rate remaining at 30%.

a5933.speaker: Economists / experts (unnamed)
a5933.name: Economists / experts (unnamed)
a5933.speech: Say the impact on Namibia will be minimal, as the US is not a key trade partner.

a5933.speaker: Klaus Schade, economist
a5933.name: Klaus Schade
a5933.title: economist
a5933.speech: Told Namibian Sun that while the reduced tariff is lower than before, it effectively ends the duty-free, quota-free access Namibia had under the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) over the past 25 years: “The USA is one of the main markets for diamonds. Tariffs are applied based on country of origin, and a certificate of origin is required - not on the point of shipment. So rerouting South African products through Namibia would be pointless and more costly.”

a5933.speaker: Klaus Schade, economist
a5933.name: Klaus Schade
a5933.title: economist
a5933.speech: Dismissed fears of product dumping in Namibia, saying: “South Africa mainly exports cars and citrus fruits to the US - goods not produced in Namibia. However, South Africa may seek new markets or expand its reach elsewhere by offering more competitive prices. Much will depend on how US importers react. Will they reduce imports, absorb costs, or pass them on to consumers?” ; added that the new tariff regime could dampen US consumer demand and contribute to global trade uncertainty, ultimately slowing economic activity worldwide.

a5933.speaker: Rodney !Hoaeb, Acting CEO of the Namibia Trade Forum
a5933.name: Rodney !Hoaeb
a5933.title: Acting CEO of the Namibia Trade Forum
a5933.speech: Echoed Schade’s sentiments; said the Southern African Customs Union (SACU) does not anticipate significant trade diversion, although there is a possibility that some goods may undergo final processing outside of South Africa: “In Namibia’s case, products reclassified as Namibian under rules of origin could save 15% if shipped from here” ; raised concerns about poultry: “Under the South Africa–US trade deal, poultry received preferential access into South Africa. With new tariffs in place, that surplus may now flood the Namibian market.”

a5933.speaker: Rodney !Hoaeb, Acting CEO of the Namibia Trade Forum
a5933.name: Rodney !Hoaeb
a5933.title: Acting CEO of the Namibia Trade Forum
a5933.speech: On the impact of the tariffs on Namibia’s green schemes, explained that agricultural imports are tightly regulated by the Agro-Marketing and Trade Agency (Amta), which only grants concessions when local supplies are depleted.

a5933.speaker: Omu Kakujaha-Matundu, economist
a5933.name: Omu Kakujaha-Matundu
a5933.title: economist
a5933.speech: Warned of indirect consequences for Namibia through the SACU revenue-sharing formula: “If South Africa lowers tariffs on US goods - either unilaterally or through SACU channels - it could reduce the overall SACU revenue pool. This would mean smaller receipts for Namibia, impacting public spending” ; added that in such a scenario, government may be forced to borrow more or impose austerity measures, which could undermine efforts to tackle unemployment.

a5933.speaker: CNN (reporting)
a5933.name: CNN (reporting)
a5933.speech: Reported that the tariff hikes are straining long-standing trade alliances.

a5933.speaker: Anna Cooban, CNN economics reporter
a5933.name: Anna Cooban
a5933.title: CNN economics reporter
a5933.speech: “Will Trump chicken out? We've seen it before. He announces tariffs, then delays or retracts them. Investors have even coined a term: TACO - Trump Always Chickens Out.”

a5950.speaker: Motseki Sebota, ex-miner (rock driller) and TB patient
a5950.name: Motseki Sebota
a5950.title: ex-miner (rock driller) and TB patient
a5950.speech: “Where I worked, I was a Rock Driller Operator.” ; “After drilling holes, we would push in explosives, then go back inside right after the blast, right into the smog and dust. When we breathed without any masks, air would sting the lungs. That dust was silica, it sticks to your lungs, and doctors later told me they were rotten.” ; “They moved me to the laundry, to wash other men’s clothes.” ; “That’s when I knew my body was finished. I had to go under TB treatment, and my breathing is no longer easy.”

a5950.speaker: Mine doctors
a5950.name: Mine doctors
a5950.speech: By 2012, found that Sebota’s lungs were “torn with holes,” forcing him out of underground work.

a5950.speaker: Dr. Llang Maama, Head of the Tuberculosis and Leprosy Department, Ministry of Health of Lesotho
a5950.name: Dr. Llang Maama
a5950.title: Head of the Tuberculosis and Leprosy Department, Ministry of Health of Lesotho
a5950.speech: Said Lesotho remains one of the world’s highest TB burden countries, with an incidence rate of 664 per 100,000 people, roughly 15,000 new cases annually, of which only 42 percent are detected and treated: “This means we are missing 58 percent of projected TB cases. Those people remain untreated and continue transmitting the infection.” ; “We have improved treatment success to around 80 percent, but the target is 90 percent. Every death reflects the weaknesses of our system.”

a5950.speaker: Dr. Llang Maama, Head of the Tuberculosis and Leprosy Department, Ministry of Health of Lesotho
a5950.name: Dr. Llang Maama
a5950.title: Head of the Tuberculosis and Leprosy Department, Ministry of Health of Lesotho
a5950.speech: On hunger and nutrition: “Sometimes it’s not even nutrition per se, but just pure hunger. When patients take medication on an empty stomach, they fail to respond to treatment.” ; “We realized this larger group also needs food. But it is costly. If you give food, you must secure enough for the household too, otherwise the patient’s ration gets eaten. It makes the program very expensive.” ; “Hunger drives non-adherence. Without nutrition, TB control remains impossible.”

a5950.speaker: Dr. Llang Maama, Head of the Tuberculosis and Leprosy Department, Ministry of Health of Lesotho
a5950.name: Dr. Llang Maama
a5950.title: Head of the Tuberculosis and Leprosy Department, Ministry of Health of Lesotho
a5950.speech: On the US funding freeze: “We lost human resources that had been recruited under US funding.” ; “There were delays in testing, and many TB patients were never followed up. It set us back in tracing the so-called ‘missing patients’.” ; “The initial uncertainty weakened confidence. Some partners paused procurement, and for months, we had testing machines without cartridges. We survived that phase, but it exposed how fragile our system is when aid shifts suddenly.”

a5950.speaker: Dr. Llang Maama, Head of the Tuberculosis and Leprosy Department, Ministry of Health of Lesotho
a5950.name: Dr. Llang Maama
a5950.title: Head of the Tuberculosis and Leprosy Department, Ministry of Health of Lesotho
a5950.speech: On ex-miners and occupational health: “Health workers and social care workers in crowded environments are also at risk. Ex-miners and their household contacts show high TB rates.” ; “We can manage only 20 clients per day. That causes delays in screening, claim processing, and treatment.”

a5950.speaker: Selibe Mochoboroane, Minister of Health of Lesotho
a5950.name: Selibe Mochoboroane
a5950.title: Minister of Health of Lesotho
a5950.speech: Acknowledged the weaknesses of the health system, pointing to fragile health infrastructure and dependence on donor aid: “Lesotho is landlocked and poor. Historically, our fathers went to South Africa to work in the mines, and that is how TB and silicosis became part of our national story.”

a5950.speaker: Selibe Mochoboroane, Minister of Health of Lesotho
a5950.name: Selibe Mochoboroane
a5950.title: Minister of Health of Lesotho
a5950.speech: On nutrition and feeding programmes: “Studies show that TB patients must get proper meals so that they can recover. We have lost people to TB because they had no food to accompany the medication.” ; “Those who cannot afford are given food and care.” ; “We are certain they can recover under those conditions.”

a5950.speaker: Selibe Mochoboroane, Minister of Health of Lesotho
a5950.name: Selibe Mochoboroane
a5950.title: Minister of Health of Lesotho
a5950.speech: On the US funding freeze and the response: “We had to revisit our budgets and cut some planned activities. Some programmes we hoped to cover, we could no longer afford. It created fear among staff and communities because they depend on those services.” ; “Through integration, we continued offering services despite reduced budgets.” ; “We brought in partners like Solidar med and Partners In Health to manage specific districts.”

a5950.speaker: Selibe Mochoboroane, Minister of Health of Lesotho
a5950.name: Selibe Mochoboroane
a5950.title: Minister of Health of Lesotho
a5950.speech: Welcomed the renewed US support as “a new dawn”: “We have begun to see an increase in TB notifications. That means more people are being found and treated. If we can sustain this effort and restore our partnerships, we will turn the corner.” ; “The resumption of support under FHI 360 and the new prevention drug come at a time when our health system needs rebuilding. We see this as a renewal of partnership, not just funding.”

a5950.speaker: Mokhothu Makhalanyane, Member of Parliament for Mokhethoaneng and chair of Parliament’s Social Cluster portfolio committee
a5950.name: Mokhothu Makhalanyane
a5950.title: Member of Parliament for Mokhethoaneng and chair of Parliament’s Social Cluster portfolio committee
a5950.speech: Said the shortage of skilled medical professionals undermines primary healthcare delivery: “You go to clinics where there’s only a nurse assistant, no doctor, not even a registered nurse. The ratio of doctors to patients is dangerously low. Without family medicine specialists in our rural facilities, we miss TB diagnoses at the community level.” ; called for structural reform: “We must strengthen family medicine, invest in rural doctors, and ensure that our people are not left in the hands of community volunteers alone.”

a5950.speaker: Mokhothu Makhalanyane, Member of Parliament for Mokhethoaneng and chair of Parliament’s Social Cluster portfolio committee
a5950.name: Mokhothu Makhalanyane
a5950.title: Member of Parliament for Mokhethoaneng and chair of Parliament’s Social Cluster portfolio committee
a5950.speech: Said the situation worsened after Lesotho lost 1.4 billion maloti in health system strengthening funds under the US-funded Millennium Challenge Account: “That was 25 percent of the health budget allocation. It was meant for primary healthcare, where these poor people live, where TB is supposed to be caught early. We lost it when the US changed its aid priorities.” ; described the situation as a “policy storm” that struck when Lesotho could least afford it: “It coincided with our poorest moment, poverty, unemployment, and rising costs of care. The cuts hit rural areas hardest, where community-based programmes are the only form of health access.”

a5950.speaker: Thomas Hines, US Chargé d’Affaires in Lesotho
a5950.name: Thomas Hines
a5950.title: US Chargé d’Affaires in Lesotho
a5950.speech: Met health minister Mochoboroane on September 15, 2025 and announced that Lesotho had been selected to receive Lenacapavir, a long-acting HIV prevention drug; said at the EpiC launch: “Together, we are advancing the fight against TB and HIV for healthier, stronger communities.”

a5950.speaker: Chris Dettweiler, US Embassy Global Health Security and Diplomacy Advisor
a5950.name: Chris Dettweiler
a5950.title: US Embassy Global Health Security and Diplomacy Advisor
a5950.speech: “FHI 360’s EPIC project will assume some of the work that was done under USAID. It supports life-saving HIV and TB care and prevention services across a big portion of the country. We’re very excited, it picks up the great work that PEPFAR has done here for nearly 20 years.” ; described Lenacapavir as a “total game-changer”: “It’s an anti-retroviral injection given every six months, shown to prevent over 99 percent of HIV infections.” ; “It’s coming to Lesotho at the same time as to Europe and North America. For a country like this, with high mobility, mineworkers, truck drivers, this is the right medication at the right time.” ; “Lesotho has made impressive gains” ; “most people living with HIV know their status and are on treatment. What has held back total control are gaps among young people and mobile populations. Lenacapavir will close that gap.” ; “This is the biggest breakthrough since the modern ARV regimens. It gives countries like Lesotho the tools to truly end the HIV epidemic, and by extension, to weaken TB.”

a6084.speaker: Tedros Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General
a6084.name: Tedros Ghebreyesus
a6084.title: WHO Director-General
a6084.speech: Made the call on Thursday in a statement outlining the critical priorities and resources needed to address 42 ongoing health emergencies, and said this includes 17 Grade 3 crises, the most severe emergencies that require the highest level of response ; “Conflict, climate change, epidemics, and displacement are converging to create an unparalleled global health crisis, with 305 million people in urgent need of humanitarian assistance in 2025” ; explained that with health systems stretched to their limits and global financial resources dwindling, the $1.5 billion is needed to help people facing the most difficult situations ; “Conflicts, outbreaks, climate-related disasters, and other health emergencies are no longer isolated or occasional; they are relentless, overlapping, and intensifying” ; “From controlling cholera outbreaks to providing mental health support in conflict zones, WHO's work extends beyond the immediate care we provide” ; stated that the appeal aimed to empower communities to protect themselves, prioritise equity, and build a legacy of preparedness ; “This appeal is about enabling WHO to save lives, protect the right to health, and provide hope where there is none. WHO is committed to delivering emergency health assistance, including in conflict zones such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the occupied Palestinian territory, and Sudan” ; outlined that WHO's response aligned with wider humanitarian efforts, prioritising essential care and medical supplies, and treating malnutrition, and added that it also includes supporting maternal and child health, conducting vaccination campaigns to prevent disease outbreaks, and offering mental health support to populations impacted by trauma ; “The appeal also highlights four key challenges facing the world: climate change, conflict, displacement, and disease outbreaks. These are responsible for fueling deeper, longer-lasting health crises and putting the world's most vulnerable at greater risk” ; said the appeal further detailed the priorities and financial needs for each of the Grade 3 emergencies that WHO was responding to, that with the support of donors and partners WHO aims to fulfil its unique role in health emergencies, and emphasised the importance of upholding the principles of international humanitarian law, ensuring that no one is left behind, even in the most challenging circumstances.

a6084.speaker: World Health Organisation (WHO)
a6084.name: World Health Organisation (WHO)
a6084.speech: Has launched a $1.5 billion Health Emergency Appeal (HEA) for 2025 to support life-saving health interventions worldwide.

a6121.speaker: USAID memo sent to contractors and partners
a6121.name: USAID memo sent to contractors and partners
a6121.speech: Instructed them to stop work immediately, as part of a broader freeze on U.S. aid and funding that began after Trump’s inauguration on January 20.

a6121.speaker: Stakeholders in the health sector
a6121.name: Stakeholders in the health sector
a6121.speech: Said the funding cut could disrupt HIV treatment, putting patients at risk of becoming ill and spreading the virus, and could also lead to the emergence of drug-resistant strains.

a6121.speaker: Kenyan government
a6121.name: Kenyan government
a6121.speech: Has urged citizens to stay calm.

a6121.speaker: Deborah Barasa, Kenyan Health Cabinet Secretary
a6121.name: Deborah Barasa
a6121.title: Kenyan Health Cabinet Secretary
a6121.speech: Says the government is exploring alternative funding after the U.S. withdrew from the World Health Organisation (WHO) and stopped HIV-related aid; speaking in Mombasa at the East Africa Health Summit, affirmed that the government is mapping out the areas most affected by Trump’s executive order, urging that Africa must build resilient health systems: “I have tasked the various state departments and programmes that will be affected by this, so that we can be able to map out and look at the impact in matters finance, human resource etc. and with this we will come with a concrete way forward in terms of interventions which we will share with the Cabinet.”

a6226.name: Dr. Adugna Deblela
a6226.title: General Director of the Ethiopian Coffee and Tea Authority

a6226.title: Chief of Party of the USAID-Feed the Future Value Chain Activity
