a6327.speaker: United Nations (UN)
a6327.name: United Nations (UN)
a6327.speech: Warned that humanitarian aid in Cabo Delgado province recorded a 15% reduction this year.

a6327.speaker: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) report
a6327.name: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) report
a6327.speech: According to an OCHA report, by the end of July some 782,000 people had received some form of support, against 923,000 in the same period of 2024, representing only 71% of the target population, estimated at 1.1 million people. ; OCHA notes that most of the assistance came from the Food Security and Livelihoods Cluster, which reached 782,000 people, but with bimonthly distributions covering only 39% of caloric needs; excluding food aid, the number of beneficiaries falls sharply to 427,000. Only 66 million dollars were mobilised against a requirement of 352 million dollars, a reduction of almost 45% compared with 2024, and the number of organisations involved fell from 78 to 56.

a6327.speaker: United Nations (UN)
a6327.name: United Nations (UN)
a6327.speech: The UN stresses that aid remains concentrated on food security, while essential areas such as shelter, health, hygiene and protection remain severely underserved.

a6373.speaker: Nobre dos Santos, Caia district administrator
a6373.name: Nobre dos Santos
a6373.title: Caia district administrator
a6373.speech: Said on Monday that nearly 100,000 people in Caia district face food insecurity, with 99,347 inhabitants food insecure, most from the villages of Chatala and Magagade in the administrative posts of Sena and Murassa; said the insecurity results from the "extreme drought" caused by El Nino and that the central government has begun to provide food assistance to more than 5,000 affected families. "However, there are still a lot of people to assist, a lot of people in need because the support isn't reaching everyone in need."

a6373.speaker: Nobre dos Santos, Caia district administrator
a6373.name: Nobre dos Santos
a6373.title: Caia district administrator
a6373.speech: Pointed to the destruction of agricultural areas by wild animals as one of the aggravating factors for the increase in hunger in the district. "The population complains about the existence of a hippopotamus that has been devastating crops at night. So we have this problem of animals all over our district."

a6373.speaker: Helder Alberto, director of the district services for economic activities, Chibabava district
a6373.name: Helder Alberto
a6373.title: director of the district services for economic activities, Chibabava district
a6373.speech: Said on Sunday that around 32,000 families are facing food insecurity due to the impacts of El Nino. "At the moment, we have around 32,000 families in a situation of food insecurity who live on remittances and the sale of small animals. The most affected area is the Goonda administrative post, our granary regarding cereal production." ; said the local government has already started to assist around 4,100 families affected by the drought, especially those in the Goonda administrative post.

a6373.speaker: United Nations Children's Fund (Unicef) (statement)
a6373.name: United Nations Children's Fund (Unicef) (statement)
a6373.speech: Recently estimated that around 4.8 million people need humanitarian assistance in Mozambique, with $64 million (EUR60.6 million) needed to meet the needs. "The multiple crises currently affecting Mozambique - conflict, drought and public health emergencies - are straining humanitarian resources. Around 4.8 million people need humanitarian assistance (10% of people with disabilities), including 3.4 million children."

a6373.speaker: United Nations (UN)
a6373.name: United Nations (UN)
a6373.speech: Said in September last year that nearly two million people needed humanitarian assistance in the country ; explained: "This year, Mozambique was affected by drought induced by the El Nino phenomenon during the 2023-2024 season. Around 1.8 million people face food insecurity between October and March 2025. Faced with this situation, the need for humanitarian assistance for the affected communities has been increasing, especially in Mozambique's central and southern regions."

a6386.speaker: Ghana Statistical Service (GSS) study, funded by UNICEF in partnership with the Korea International Cooperation Agency and USAID
a6386.name: Ghana Statistical Service (GSS) study
a6386.title: funded by UNICEF in partnership with the Korea International Cooperation Agency and USAID
a6386.speech: Has shown that nine out of 10 districts in the Ashanti Region have the highest rates of underage sex among females ; the report indicated that adolescent girls aged 16 to 19 had sex before the age of 16 years ; showed that on a national scale, all 10 districts with the highest percentage of adolescent boys engaging in underage sex were in the Eastern Region, of which about one in every three adolescent boys aged 16 to 19 had sex before 16 years, the highest district being Upper Manya Krobo, followed by Atiwa West, Upper West Akim, and others, while the lowest was recorded in the North East Gonja, Mion, and Mamprugu Moagduri districts.

a6386.speaker: Ghana Statistical Service (GSS) report
a6386.name: Ghana Statistical Service (GSS) report
a6386.speech: Revealed that districts in the Bono and Western North regions had districts in the top 10 with the highest prevalence of multiple sexual partners among adolescent girls, and that all districts except one in the top 10 that recorded the highest rate of multiple sexual partnerships among adolescent boys were in the Oti Region, led by the Guan, Nkwanta South, and Krachi Nchumuru districts.

a6386.speaker: Ghana Statistical Service (GSS) report on the Utilisation of Maternal Health Care Services
a6386.name: Ghana Statistical Service (GSS) report on the Utilisation of Maternal Health Care Services
a6386.speech: Revealed that five of the districts in the top 10 are in the Upper East Region, with districts in the Northern, Savannah, North East, and Savanna with one or more districts in the bottom 10; in these districts, less than half of women had four or more antenatal care visits, facility delivery, and postnatal care.

a6386.speaker: Dr Peter Takyi Peprah, Director of Methods and Standards Directorates, Ghana Statistical Service
a6386.name: Dr Peter Takyi Peprah
a6386.title: Director of Methods and Standards Directorates, Ghana Statistical Service
a6386.speech: Presented the report on the topic: “Adolescent Risky Sexual Behaviour and Utilisation of Maternal Health Services”.

a6386.speaker: Dr Athanasius Ayetey Larbi, Gynaecologist, Ghana Health Service
a6386.name: Dr Athanasius Ayetey Larbi
a6386.title: Gynaecologist, Ghana Health Service
a6386.speech: Said the report would help authorities to make interventions to address the challenges faced by adolescent girls and boys' sexual behaviours ; said progress had been made nationally but the persistent intraregional disparities required intensified focus in the districts that were performing relatively worse than others.

a6473.speaker: Cristian Munduate, UNICEF’s representative in Nigeria
a6473.name: Cristian Munduate
a6473.title: UNICEF’s representative in Nigeria
a6473.speech: Emphasised the transformative power of the media in influencing policy, public perception, and urgent action to improve children’s lives, urging the media to leverage its platforms to improve the lives of Nigeria’s 110 million children: “Media can drive change by keeping children’s issues at the top of the national agenda” ; argued that they must move beyond reporting daily events to deliberate, sustained advocacy that holds stakeholders accountable: “This includes the federal and state governments, religious and traditional leaders, and families. You are uniquely positioned to inform and equip these stakeholders with the tools to protect children’s rights” ; cited past examples where media pressure influenced government action, such as stepping in to protect children from harsh judicial punishments ; challenged media organizations to celebrate progress and positive developments for children while maintaining a focus on the urgent need for reforms in education, healthcare, and poverty alleviation ; “Childhood is short—just 18 years. The changes we make today are the only ones that matter for these children. The media has the power to create a sense of urgency and push for the immediate actions that children cannot wait for” ; encouraged media to foster competition among states in achieving milestones like open defecation-free status and improving access to food and education, affirming that by amplifying solutions and inspiring collaboration, the media can change the narrative for Nigeria’s children and help secure their future.

a6473.speaker: Cristian Munduate, UNICEF’s representative in Nigeria (on child poverty statistics)
a6473.name: Cristian Munduate
a6473.title: UNICEF’s representative in Nigeria (on child poverty statistics)
a6473.speech: Noted that nearly half of Nigerian children live in poverty, with 67 percent experiencing multidimensional deprivations such as malnutrition, lack of education, and inadequate healthcare; additionally, 2.1 million children remain unvaccinated, 4.9 million need urgent humanitarian aid, and three out of four children in school are failing to meet basic literacy and numeracy standards.

a6473.speaker: 2024 Situational Analysis of Children and Adolescents in Nigeria (report)
a6473.name: 2024 Situational Analysis of Children and Adolescents in Nigeria (report)
a6473.speech: Showed that nearly half of all Nigerian children live in poverty; stated that 41 out of every 1,000 newborns die before their first birthday, and 2.1 million children remain unvaccinated; additionally, 4.9 million children are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance, while 40 percent of children under five are stunted due to malnutrition, and eight percent suffer from wasting.

a6473.speaker: Eze Anaba, president, Nigerian Guild of Editors (NGE)
a6473.name: Eze Anaba
a6473.title: president, Nigerian Guild of Editors (NGE)
a6473.speech: Urged media practitioners to take a more proactive role in advocating for the rights and well-being of Nigerian children, underscoring the urgent need to address pressing issues affecting children, including malnutrition, lack of education, and vulnerability to preventable diseases: “Children in Nigeria are still dying from diseases that have been eradicated elsewhere or for which vaccinations are available. This situation demands a collective effort from media practitioners, health workers, policymakers, and the government to declare a state of emergency for children and place them at the forefront of national priorities.”

a6659.speaker: Amnesty International
a6659.name: Amnesty International
a6659.speech: Issued a stark warning about a rapidly worsening global human rights crisis, attributing the acceleration of repressive global trends to what it describes as the "Trump effect" - a broad and deliberate assault on international law and human rights by the United States under President Donald Trump's second administration.

a6659.speaker: Amnesty International, annual report "The State of the World's Human Rights"
a6659.name: Amnesty International
a6659.title: annual report "The State of the World's Human Rights"
a6659.speech: Reviewing conditions in 150 countries throughout 2024, depicts a world sliding deeper into authoritarianism, saying governments are increasingly silencing dissent, curtailing fundamental freedoms and undermining accountability mechanisms while multilateral systems built to protect human rights are being steadily dismantled: "Year after year, we have warned of the dangers of human rights backsliding. But events of the past 12 months - not least Israel's livestreamed but unheeded genocide of Palestinians in Gaza - have laid bare just how hellish the world can be for so many when the most powerful states jettison international law and disregard multilateral institutions."

a6659.speaker: Agnes Callamard, Amnesty International Secretary General
a6659.name: Agnes Callamard
a6659.title: Amnesty International Secretary General
a6659.speech: Described Trump's return to power as a catalyst for global regression, saying his administration has exhibited outright contempt for universal rights and has deliberately dismantled key institutions meant to safeguard justice, equality and the environment; by attacking racial and gender justice, rolling back climate action, defunding global health efforts and undermining asylum systems, Trump has created a permissive atmosphere for other anti-rights actors around the world to intensify their own crackdowns.

a6659.speaker: Amnesty International
a6659.name: Amnesty International
a6659.speech: "One hundred days into his second term, President Trump has shown only utter contempt for universal human rights."

a6659.speaker: Amnesty International (report)
a6659.name: Amnesty International (report)
a6659.speech: Emphasised that the crisis cannot be blamed on one leader alone, saying the world has been witnessing a long, creeping rise in authoritarian practices driven by both aspiring and elected leaders who view power as a means to crush dissent and enrich elites, and warning that entire governments are now weaponizing the law to sow fear and evade scrutiny; documented widespread suppression of civil society through arbitrary arrests, censorship and criminalization of activists, human rights defenders and journalists.

a6659.speaker: Amnesty International (report)
a6659.name: Amnesty International (report)
a6659.speech: Documented violent responses to public protests and unrest across numerous countries, describing brutal state-led crackdowns and abuses including excessive and often lethal force against demonstrators; noted that security forces used repression as a tool to crush civil disobedience, leaving thousands dead or injured, while peaceful protestors faced indefinite detention under vaguely worded anti-terror laws.

a6659.speaker: Amnesty International (report)
a6659.name: Amnesty International (report)
a6659.speech: Accused powerful states of allowing war crimes and other serious violations of international law - particularly atrocities in Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan and Myanmar - to persist unchecked, while international responses remained inconsistent and in many cases absent; said the Trump administration's suspension of foreign aid and its imposition of sanctions on international justice bodies exacerbated humanitarian conditions in multiple regions and undermined global efforts to hold perpetrators accountable.

a6659.speaker: Amnesty International (report)
a6659.name: Amnesty International (report)
a6659.speech: Highlighted how collective failures to address the climate crisis, growing inequality and corporate excess are condemning future generations to greater hardship; described the 2024 COP29 summit as a failure, with fossil fuel interests dominating the agenda and wealthy nations pushing through inadequate financing deals that left poorer countries vulnerable, and saw Trump's withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and his aggressive promotion of fossil fuel extraction as not only regressive but dangerously influential.

a6659.speaker: Amnesty International (report)
a6659.name: Amnesty International (report)
a6659.speech: Said rising economic inequality was another major theme, as governments allowed unchecked corporate power, failed to regulate financial abuses and scapegoated migrants and refugees to deflect blame for deepening poverty and stagnation, and said such rhetoric, often laced with racism and xenophobia, is helping normalize exclusionary politics while deflecting from the real drivers of inequality.

a6659.speaker: Amnesty International (report)
a6659.name: Amnesty International (report)
a6659.speech: Expressed grave concern over attacks on women, girls and LGBTI people, noting a worsening global backlash against gender rights, and said the Trump administration has played a central role in this trend by dismantling gender-focused programs, attacking transgender rights and halting funding for services benefiting women and girls worldwide.

a6659.speaker: Amnesty International (report)
a6659.name: Amnesty International (report)
a6659.speech: Warned of the growing misuse of technology by states and corporations, with surveillance tools entrenching discrimination and artificial intelligence systems reinforcing existing inequalities, and criticised the Trump administration's cozy relationship with tech billionaires, accusing it of rolling back regulatory safeguards and encouraging platforms to weaken content moderation and allow disinformation, hate speech and corporate influence to proliferate.

a6659.speaker: Amnesty International (report)
a6659.name: Amnesty International (report)
a6659.speech: Commended the resilience of multilateral bodies like the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice, which took significant steps in 2024 to pursue accountability for war crimes and other serious violations, and noted growing leadership from countries in the Global South, including legal challenges, arms embargo initiatives and international cooperation aimed at restoring the rule of law; concluded by urging governments to act boldly and collectively to reverse the damage, restore international justice and protect the fundamental rights of all people.

a6659.speaker: Agnes Callamard, Amnesty International Secretary General
a6659.name: Agnes Callamard
a6659.title: Amnesty International Secretary General
a6659.speech: Emphasised that while the current landscape is bleak, the erosion of human rights is not irreversible, noting that around the world people continue to resist, mobilize and vote against anti-rights regimes and that civil society, despite facing threats and restrictions, remains a powerful force.

a6662.speaker: Various stakeholders at the Research and Innovation Week at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6662.name: Various stakeholders at the Research and Innovation Week at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6662.speech: Said that an increase in financial resources, the improvement of infrastructure and of ICT skills among young people, and cooperation between universities, the private sector and development stakeholders are among the things that will help improve the research and innovation carried out in the country, and that innovators, researchers and the community should benefit from it.

a6662.speaker: Professor William Anangisye, Vice Chancellor of the University of Dar es Salaam
a6662.name: Professor William Anangisye
a6662.title: Vice Chancellor of the University of Dar es Salaam
a6662.speech: Pointed out that a shortage of financial resources and weak links with the industrial sector have been causing a deadlock in the commercialisation of research and innovations produced in the country, and said commercialisation is a broad process requiring a good environment, sufficient funding, strategic advice and private sector participation: "The gap between university research and its implementation in the industrial and business sector is a challenge that requires genuine cooperation between higher education institutions, the private sector, the Government and investors." ; said the aim is to ensure innovative products reach the market, create jobs, improve the lives of Tanzanians and contribute substantially to national development, and urged private sector stakeholders and investors to keep cooperating with researchers and to provide advice and capital to turn innovative ideas into businesses and services.

a6662.speaker: Professor Lilian Kaale, lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6662.name: Professor Lilian Kaale
a6662.title: lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6662.speech: Said it is difficult to achieve such success without robust systems of sustainable financing and intellectual property management, and advised that through research and innovation units innovators and researchers be educated and sensitised about intellectual property rights in order to protect the results of their work: "That education is important to help them protect their innovations as well as their research, so it is important for them to have sufficient understanding of how they can put protection on their work."

a6662.speaker: Peter Ulanga, Chief Executive Officer of Air Tanzania Company Limited (ATCL)
a6662.name: Peter Ulanga
a6662.title: Chief Executive Officer of Air Tanzania Company Limited (ATCL)
a6662.speech: Stressed greater investment in technology in order to achieve a major revolution in research and innovation in the country.

a6662.speaker: Professor Kitila Mkumbo, Tanzanian Minister of Planning and Investment
a6662.name: Professor Kitila Mkumbo
a6662.title: Tanzanian Minister of Planning and Investment
a6662.speech: Stressed cooperation between educational institutions and the private sector in order to help produce research and innovations that bring solutions to the challenges facing society, and said the Government is determined to ensure that research and innovation become important tools for economic and social development alongside building a nation led by knowledge: "The research and innovations carried out in the country should not remain only on paper or in academic journals, but should make a direct contribution to the lives of Tanzanians." ; added that the Government has put money into ensuring innovations and research have positive results, so it is time to look at how they can reach the market.

a6703.speaker: Aflodis Kagaba, executive director of the Health Development Initiative
a6703.name: Aflodis Kagaba
a6703.title: executive director of the Health Development Initiative
a6703.speech: "Maybe the government has tangible reasons for doing this... but we need to find a sustainable solution to funding."

a6703.speaker: Rwanda and Belgium
a6703.name: Rwanda and Belgium
a6703.speech: Vowed residents and businesses would not face serious consequences from the diplomatic breakdown.

a6703.speaker: Official at Rwanda's education ministry (anonymous)
a6703.name: Official at Rwanda's education ministry (anonymous)
a6703.speech: Said the government is effectively "telling the school to pack up and close" ; "It is unfathomable that such a reputable and historical international school will adopt a Rwandan curriculum."

a6703.speaker: Phil Clark, international politics professor at London's School of Oriental and African Studies
a6703.name: Phil Clark
a6703.title: international politics professor at London's School of Oriental and African Studies
a6703.speech: Said cuts to healthcare and education projects will have an impact, but the government will likely find alternative funding ; "Paradoxically, this may incentivise the Rwandan state to seek greater mineral wealth from eastern Congo to cover any shortfall in foreign donor assistance." ; added the biggest impact would be Rwanda's loss of lobbying power in the European Union, which is headquartered in Belgium.

a6703.speaker: Louis Gitinywa, lawyer and political analyst
a6703.name: Louis Gitinywa
a6703.title: lawyer and political analyst
a6703.speech: Said Rwanda was "not as clean as wool" in the dispute, but he agreed with the government's tough stance ; "Rwanda is a small country, but it is a state, and it shouldn't be bullied." ; "For many decades, Belgium has been (the) fuelling fire for its strategic interests in the region." ; said many countries were taking advantage of the chaos in the DRC: "Why should Rwanda be punished for it when it has legitimate security justifications to be in DRC?"

a6703.speaker: Louis Gitinywa, lawyer and political analyst
a6703.name: Louis Gitinywa
a6703.title: lawyer and political analyst
a6703.speech: Said Kigali must engage constructively with its critics: "Rwanda needs to do more than call Belgians names. We need a long-term plan to soften the effects of the sanctions."

a6703.speaker: Kigali (Rwandan government)
a6703.name: Kigali (Rwandan government)
a6703.speech: Argues it is threatened by DRC-based armed groups founded by ethnic Hutu leaders who carried out the 1994 genocide of the Tutsis in Rwanda.

a6798.speaker: Federal Supreme Court Justices (Ethiopia)
a6798.name: Federal Supreme Court Justices (Ethiopia)
a6798.speech: Three weeks ago set the final period on the longest-running white collar case, throwing out every count and confirming an earlier acquittal by judges at the Federal High Court.

a6798.speaker: Temesgen Yilma, businessman and defendant
a6798.name: Temesgen Yilma
a6798.title: businessman and defendant
a6798.speech: “Justice, however late, will find its way around,” calling the judgment “a long overdue vindication.”

a6798.speaker: Haileyesus Mengistu, former majority shareholder of Cosmo Trading Plc
a6798.name: Haileyesus Mengistu
a6798.title: former majority shareholder of Cosmo Trading Plc
a6798.speech: Later told federal officials the share transfer had been extorted, claiming Azeb's entourage had muscled its way into the negotiations, subjected him to “duress and physical harassment,” and walked off with corporate documents; according to his complaint, Cosmo Trading's new owners then used the company as a funnel, drawing bank loans in the company's name, siphoning the cash to related entities, and laundering a portion through the parallel forex market; he wrote to then Attorney General Adanech Abiebie, now mayor of Addis Abeba, pleading for help.

a6798.speaker: Court records
a6798.name: Court records
a6798.speech: Show that part of the consideration was the commercial property that bankers pegged at 50 million Br.

a6798.speaker: State prosecutors (Ethiopia)
a6798.name: State prosecutors (Ethiopia)
a6798.speech: In 2019 filed a 29 page charge sheet naming four individuals, Azeb, Temesgen, Mesfin Asmamaw, Cosmo Trading's former general manager, and an associate, as well as three companies, JJ Property, TTH Trading and Boston Real Estate; charged that 61 million Br was taken as working capital loan and a 10 million Br short term facility from Awash Bank; 21 million Br applied to clear Cosmo Trading's old debts; 32.5 million Br routed to JJ Property; seven million Birr to Boston Real Estate; and 16 million Br covering TTH's liabilities; accused Temesgen of pocketing 14.4 million Br in rent from the hotel and another 1.4 million Br from selling a grader. A separate file alleged that four of the defendants ran an underground remittance service, swapping Birr in Addis Abeba for foreign currency parked in Europe and the U.S.

a6798.speaker: Defence lawyers
a6798.name: Defence lawyers
a6798.speech: Denied every allegation, calling the money movements “ordinary internal transfers of a company drowning in more than 40 million Br of legacy debt”; cited an earlier civil judgment that upheld the share sale as valid and appealed to judges that the prosecution was bound to prove criminal intent beyond a reasonable doubt.

a6798.speaker: Federal High Court panel — Judges Adem Seid, Yenenesh Bahiru and Imiru Tolera
a6798.name: Federal High Court panel — Judges Adem Seid
a6798.title: Yenenesh Bahiru and Imiru Tolera
a6798.speech: Found the defence argument persuasive; on April 16 dismissed the first count, a compound allegation of breach of trust and money laundering, before asking the defence to present a single exhibit, saying prosecutors had not even shown the existence of a predicate offence.

a6798.speaker: Haileyesus Mengistu, former majority shareholder of Cosmo Trading Plc
a6798.name: Haileyesus Mengistu
a6798.title: former majority shareholder of Cosmo Trading Plc
a6798.speech: “I was robbed of my right and property,” vowing to appeal.

a6798.speaker: Supreme Court (civil case)
a6798.name: Supreme Court (civil case)
a6798.speech: Reinstated the share transfer deal after finding gaps in the alleged duress and noting that some tax clearances were missing, a clerical oversight the judges called curable.

a6798.speaker: Yared Seyoum, criminal lawyer who followed the proceedings
a6798.name: Yared Seyoum
a6798.title: criminal lawyer who followed the proceedings
a6798.speech: Said prosecutors bear the greatest responsibility to explain the case: “Defendants can remain silent unless the state produces airtight evidence” ; “The prosecution's narrative did not connect the dots.”

a6798.speaker: Melaku Michael, prosecutor and deputy director for economic crimes, Ministry of Justice
a6798.name: Melaku Michael
a6798.title: prosecutor and deputy director for economic crimes, Ministry of Justice
a6798.speech: Told Fortune his team is combing through the docket to decide whether to appeal to the Court of Cassation: “We'll be thoroughly evaluating the presented materials alongside the legal documents and witness testimonies and decide whether to appeal within a month.”

a6798.speaker: Legal experts
a6798.name: Legal experts
a6798.speech: Say money laundering charges require proof that the defendants concealed proceeds of a separate crime; say the affair uncovers Ethiopia's fragile corporate governance plumbing, noting share transfers often rely on private agreements notarised before being lodged with the Ministry of Trade, which maintains no realtime public register; warn that prolonged litigation may spook wouldbe entrants over contract administrations and dispute resolution.

a6798.speaker: Temesgen Yilma, businessman and defendant
a6798.name: Temesgen Yilma
a6798.title: businessman and defendant
a6798.speech: According to him, Cosmo Trading's balance sheet was “on life support” when JJ Property and TTH Trading stepped in, and every Birr transferred to sister companies covered payroll, suppliers or emergency maintenance that kept the property open ; “We were merely taking back what we had invested” ; “It's been a huge distraction, emotionally and financially.”

a6798.speaker: Haileyesus Mengistu, former majority shareholder of Cosmo Trading Plc
a6798.name: Haileyesus Mengistu
a6798.title: former majority shareholder of Cosmo Trading Plc
a6798.speech: Insists the fight is far from over; pressed his claim that he never saw most of the money agreed to transfer his shares and that signatures acknowledging payment were forged; disputes the valuation of the property, claiming it is worth at least 250 million Br rather than the 60 million Br in one contract; argued the criminal and civil files should have been merged from the start; says he will pursue every forum until he recovers what he calls “stolen property” ; “An unfair judgment has been made.”

a6815.speaker: Save the Children Situation report (December)
a6815.name: Save the Children Situation report (December)
a6815.speech: According to a Save the Children Situation report that came out in December, levels of humanitarian need are extremely high given that most displaced people from the armed conflict along the Somali/Oromia border are already in drought affected zones. According to the overview of the report on the situation, displaced people live in approximately 100 sites in addition to those in host communities. It also states that displaced people in many locations are frustrated that numerous assessments have been carried out without humanitarian assistance.

a6815.speaker: Government of Ethiopia (as quoted in the Save the Children report)
a6815.name: Government of Ethiopia (as quoted in the Save the Children report)
a6815.speech: “The government therefore urges humanitarian agencies not to carry out verification assessment exercises unless they can ensure humanitarian assistance follows immediately as the current coverage is very little and a vast majority of internally displaced people are not receiving assistance in the ongoing collective response,” it reads.

a6815.speaker: Recent multi-agency team assessment
a6815.name: Recent multi-agency team assessment
a6815.speech: An assessment of humanitarian needs, vulnerability and potential risks clearly indicated the need for life-saving interventions for food security, emergency shelters, WASH, health, nutrition, education and child protection needs. The findings of the assessment also show that cumulative effects of the drought and conflict-induced displacement is adding further stress to food reserves and water sources.

a6815.speaker: Save the Children
a6815.name: Save the Children
a6815.speech: Although no official statistics are available on the number of people dead or seriously injured on both sides, many women and children and elderly are believed to have been affected, Save the Children says. In many Kebeles and villages that were attacked, houses were burned, assets and personal belongings looted, and community assets destroyed, including looting of schools, health centers and mill houses.

a6815.speaker: Ethiopia’s National Disaster Risk Management and Food Security Sector (report)
a6815.name: Ethiopia’s National Disaster Risk Management and Food Security Sector (report)
a6815.speech: The recent report estimated that 929,000 people; 600,000 in Oromia and 329,000 in Somalia, have been displaced due to the border conflict between the two ethnic groups that started in April 2017 and escalated in late September 2017.

a6815.speaker: Save the Children (the humanitarian agency)
a6815.name: Save the Children (the humanitarian agency)
a6815.speech: According to the humanitarian agency, there are reportedly a significant number of malnourished children, pregnant girls due to child marriage, children with physical and mental disabilities, physical injuries, separated and unaccompanied children, and children with deteriorating physiological situations. Most of school age children of displaced communities are not attending school since there is no established emergency school at many of the displaced people sites.

a6857.speaker: Chinese government (Beijing)
a6857.name: Chinese government (Beijing)
a6857.speech: Said China sent an 82-person team of rescuers to Myanmar on Saturday.

a6857.speaker: Chinese state media
a6857.name: Chinese state media
a6857.speech: Said a separate rescue team arrived in Myanmar’s commercial hub Yangon on Saturday.

a6857.speaker: China’s international aid agency
a6857.name: China’s international aid agency
a6857.speech: Said Saturday that the Chinese government will also provide Myanmar with 100 million yuan (US$13.8 million) in emergency humanitarian assistance, with shipments to begin today.

a6857.speaker: Government of Hong Kong (statement)
a6857.name: Government of Hong Kong (statement)
a6857.speech: Said a 51-person team from Hong Kong has arrived in Myanmar, that the city also sent two search and rescue dogs and equipment including life detectors, and that it has earmarked HK$30 million (US$3.8 million) for emergency relief support to Myanmar.

a6857.speaker: Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, Indian foreign minister
a6857.name: Subrahmanyam Jaishankar
a6857.title: Indian foreign minister
a6857.speech: Said a military transport plane had been dispatched carrying hygiene kits, blankets and food parcels. “A search and rescue team and medical team is also accompanying this flight.”

a6857.speaker: Indian officials (unnamed)
a6857.name: Indian officials (unnamed)
a6857.speech: Said four more aircraft were being sent with personnel and equipment, as well as two navy ships.

a6857.speaker: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
a6857.name: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
a6857.speech: Launched an emergency appeal for more than US$100 million to help 100,000 people with life-saving relief.

a6857.speaker: UN humanitarian agency OCHA (statement)
a6857.name: UN humanitarian agency OCHA (statement)
a6857.speech: “A severe shortage of medical supplies is hampering response efforts, including trauma kits, blood bags, anaesthetics, assistive devices, essential medicines and tents for health workers.”

a6857.speaker: US President Donald Trump
a6857.name: US President Donald Trump
a6857.speech: Vowed Washington would assist Myanmar, describing the quake as “terrible”: “It’s a real bad one, and we will be helping. We’ve already spoken with the country,” he told reporters.

a6857.speaker: European Union
a6857.name: European Union
a6857.speech: Said it was providing 2.5 million euros (US$2.7 million) in initial emergency aid, and assessing the needs on the ground in order to mobilise further assistance.

a6857.speaker: Britain / Jennifer Chapman, UK development minister
a6857.name: Britain / Jennifer Chapman
a6857.title: UK development minister
a6857.speech: Britain pledged £10 million (US$12.9 million) in humanitarian aid, with development minister Jennifer Chapman saying UK-funded local partners were already mobilising on the ground.

a6857.speaker: Government of Ireland
a6857.name: Government of Ireland
a6857.speech: Announced it would contribute an initial six million euros in aid, with half going to Red Cross organisations and the other half to United Nations’ agencies.

a6857.speaker: Malaysia’s foreign ministry
a6857.name: Malaysia’s foreign ministry
a6857.speech: Said it would send a team to Myanmar consisting of one commander and 49 rescue personnel “to support ongoing humanitarian and disaster relief operations”.

a6857.speaker: Government of Indonesia
a6857.name: Government of Indonesia
a6857.speech: Said it will send a search and rescue team, medical team and logistical aid to Myanmar, starting today.

a6857.speaker: Kristomei Sianturi, Indonesian military spokesman
a6857.name: Kristomei Sianturi
a6857.title: Indonesian military spokesman
a6857.speech: Reported by local media as saying the Indonesian military will send a hospital ship, three Hercules aircraft and four helicopters to assist emergency response.

a6857.speaker: Government of the Philippines
a6857.name: Government of the Philippines
a6857.speech: Said Saturday it is sending a team of 114 people, including medics, firefighters and members of the armed forces, with a tentative deployment date of Tuesday.

a6857.speaker: Government of Vietnam
a6857.name: Government of Vietnam
a6857.speech: Said it would send 80 rescuers to help search and recovery efforts.

a6857.speaker: Public Security Ministry (Vietnam), via a ministry-run newspaper
a6857.name: Public Security Ministry (Vietnam)
a6857.title: via a ministry-run newspaper
a6857.speech: Said it will send a team of police officers and medics, all to be deployed yesterday.

a6857.speaker: Government of South Korea
a6857.name: Government of South Korea
a6857.speech: Said it would send US$2 million in humanitarian assistance “to support urgent rescue and relief efforts” after the earthquake.

a6857.speaker: Government of New Zealand
a6857.name: Government of New Zealand
a6857.speech: Said it would give NZ$2.0 million (US$1.1 million) to the International Red Cross for the emergency response.

a6928.speaker: Ally Harith, researcher and analyst of education affairs and Kiswahili language expert from Zanzibar
a6928.name: Ally Harith
a6928.title: researcher and analyst of education affairs and Kiswahili language expert from Zanzibar
a6928.speech: Argues that when the vocabulary of a language is not used in its proper place it can either distort or completely fail to deliver the message intended by the writer or speaker; that if you examine the news, features and even advertisements of many media outlets you will find many errors in the use of standard and eloquent language, including poor use of some vocabulary, a matter which, despite being complained about daily, still appears to afflict the news industry in the country and sometimes even international media outlets; that for journalists language is not merely a part of their work to be given low status, but rather the tool, the capital and the treasure of their work; that poor attention to language may be caused by contempt, weak language proficiency and sometimes the absence of dedicated language editors in many if not all media houses; and that "It is a duty that admits no excuse for journalists to have the desire, the interest and the personal passion to learn the foundations, procedures and rules of language," so that their work is of high quality and conveys what it is intended to convey.

a6928.speaker: DW Kiswahili (news item posted on the outlet's Facebook account, 21 January 2025)
a6928.name: DW Kiswahili (news item posted on the outlet's Facebook account
a6928.title: 21 January 2025)
a6928.speech: "Donald Trump tayari ameanza kazi kama rais wa 47 wa Marekani..." ("Donald Trump has already begun work as/like the 47th president of the United States...") - which the author says contains an incorrect use of the conjunction 'kama' and should have read "Donald Trump tayari ameanza kazi akiwa rais wa 47 wa Marekani..."

a6928.speaker: Tanzania Broadcasting Corporation (TBConline, Facebook post, 9 February 2025)
a6928.name: Tanzania Broadcasting Corporation (TBConline
a6928.title: Facebook post, 9 February 2025)
a6928.speech: "Aidha amesema mashindano hayo mbali na kuwa yanachochea usomaji wa Qur'aan Tukufu pia hujenga uelewa wa hofu ya Mwenyezi Mungu lakini pia yanaitangaza Tanzania katika taswira chanya." ("Furthermore he said that the competition, besides encouraging the reading of the Holy Qur'an, also builds an understanding of the fear of Almighty God but also promotes Tanzania in a positive image.")

a6928.speaker: Dr Doto Biteko, Deputy Prime Minister of Tanzania (reported by TBC)
a6928.name: Dr Doto Biteko
a6928.title: Deputy Prime Minister of Tanzania (reported by TBC)
a6928.speech: Said, while launching the International Holy Qur'an Competition on 9 February 2025, that the competition encourages the reading of the Holy Qur'an, builds an understanding of the fear of Almighty God, and promotes Tanzania in a positive image.

a7011.speaker: Donald Trump, US President (post on Truth Social)
a7011.name: Donald Trump
a7011.title: US President (post on Truth Social)
a7011.speech: Threatened to suspend all future United States aid to South Africa because of Pretoria's land expropriation policy, promising to cut funding until an investigation is carried out into allegations that "certain classes" of people are being mistreated by the Pretoria authorities. "South Africa is confiscating land and treating certain classes of people VERY BADLY. The United States will not tolerate this, we will act" ; "I will cut off all future funding to South Africa until a full investigation of this situation has been completed!"

a7011.speaker: South African government / the Presidency (communique received by APA)
a7011.name: South African government / the Presidency (communique received by APA)
a7011.speech: Stated that South Africa is a constitutional democracy deeply rooted in the rule of law, justice and equality, and refuses to confiscate land: "the recently adopted expropriation law is not an instrument of confiscation, but a legal process mandated by the Constitution that guarantees public access to land in an equitable and just manner, as provided for by the Constitution. South Africa, like the United States of America and other countries, has always had expropriation laws that balance the need for public use of land and the protection of the rights of landowners." ; said it was looking forward to engaging with the Trump administration on land reform policy and on questions of bilateral interest: "We are confident that through these engagements we will share a better common understanding on these issues."

a7032.speaker: Merriam-Webster online dictionary
a7032.name: Merriam-Webster online dictionary
a7032.speech: Categorizes hate speech as a noun referring to speech that expresses hatred toward a particular group of people.

a7032.speaker: Cambridge online dictionary
a7032.name: Cambridge online dictionary
a7032.speech: Defines it as public speech that expresses hate or encourages violence toward a person or group based on characteristics such as race, religion, sex, or sexual orientation.

a7032.speaker: United Nations Strategy and Plan of Action on Hate Speech
a7032.name: United Nations Strategy and Plan of Action on Hate Speech
a7032.speech: Defines hate speech as “any kind of communication in speech, writing or behaviour, that attacks or uses pejorative or discriminatory language with reference to a person or a group on the basis of who they are, in other words, based on their religion, ethnicity, nationality, race, colour, descent, gender or other identity factor.”

a7032.speaker: Council of Europe
a7032.name: Council of Europe
a7032.speech: Hate speech is understood as all types of expression that incite, promote, spread or justify violence, hatred or discrimination against a person or group of persons, or that denigrates them, by reason of their real or attributed personal characteristics or status such as “race”, colour, language, religion, nationality, national or ethnic origin, age, disability, sex, gender identity and sexual orientation.

a7032.speaker: Article 19
a7032.name: Article 19
a7032.speech: Describes hate speech as an “emotive concept [with] no universally accepted definition”; a term used to describe broad discourse that is extremely negative and constitutes a threat to social peace.

a7032.speaker: Pippa Norris (2014)
a7032.name: Pippa Norris (2014)
a7032.speech: Emphasizes the importance of maintaining political legitimacy and adhering to global democratic standards, noting that deviations can undermine the integrity of democratic systems.

a7032.speaker: Steven Levitsky and Daniel Ziblatt (2018), “How Democracies Die”
a7032.name: Steven Levitsky and Daniel Ziblatt (2018)
a7032.title: “How Democracies Die”
a7032.speech: Discuss how political actors who treat rivals as enemies and intimidate the free press contribute to the weakening of democratic institutions.

a7032.speaker: UN Report (2011)
a7032.name: UN Report (2011)
a7032.speech: Documented that Kenya's 2007–2008 post-election violence resulted in the deaths of over 1,100 people and the displacement of more than 600,000 others, with targeted killings, sexual violence and destruction of property as ethnic rivalries were exacerbated by inflammatory rhetoric from political leaders ; that Côte d'Ivoire's 2010–2011 post-election crisis led to the deaths of approximately 3,000 people, the raping of over 150 women and the displacement of more than one million, with hate speech playing a central role in fuelling tensions ; and that Rwanda's 1994 genocide, in which radio broadcasts and political propaganda encouraged ethnic hatred, culminated in the mass killing of over 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus in just 100 days.

a7032.speaker: Yahya Jammeh, former President of The Gambia
a7032.name: Yahya Jammeh
a7032.title: former President of The Gambia
a7032.speech: At a political rally in Tallinding in June 2016 referred to the Mandinka ethnic group as “enemies, foreigners” and threatened to kill them one by one, vowing to place them “where even a fly cannot see them”; frequently used public platforms to brand political opponents as “traitors” and “enemies of the state”, often targeting specific ethnic groups to stoke fear and loyalty among his supporters.

a7032.speaker: Human Rights Watch (2016)
a7032.name: Human Rights Watch (2016)
a7032.speech: Documented Jammeh's June 2016 Tallinding rally remarks describing the Mandinka ethnic group as “enemies, foreigners” and threatening to kill them one by one.

a7032.speaker: Amnesty International (2016)
a7032.name: Amnesty International (2016)
a7032.speech: The 2016 death of Solo Sandeng, an opposition activist arrested and killed in custody after leading a protest for electoral reform, underscores the “lethal consequences of Jammeh's regime and its hate-driven propaganda.”

a7032.speaker: Paradigm Initiative (2021 report)
a7032.name: Paradigm Initiative (2021 report)
a7032.speech: Confirmed that much of the hate speech in The Gambia, which is usually ethnic or political in nature, occurs on social media platforms like Meta (Facebook) and WhatsApp, and highlighted how political supporters use these platforms to target opponents with derogatory language, false accusations and incitements to violence, often under the cloak of anonymity.

a7032.speaker: Malagen (2023 media monitoring report)
a7032.name: Malagen (2023 media monitoring report)
a7032.speech: Underscored the prevalence of hate speech on social media, noting that political supporters frequently use these platforms to disseminate inflammatory content.

a7032.speaker: International Republican Institute (2021)
a7032.name: International Republican Institute (2021)
a7032.speech: Reported that during the 2021 presidential election campaign supporters of the ruling National People's Party (NPP) and the opposition United Democratic Party (UDP) engaged in online vitriol, with some posts inciting violence against perceived political or ethnic adversaries.

a7032.speaker: African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance (ACDEG) (African Union, 2007)
a7032.name: African Charter on Democracy
a7032.title: Elections and Governance (ACDEG) (African Union, 2007)
a7032.speech: Underscores the responsibility of member states to prevent incitement to violence and discrimination, particularly during electoral processes, as a means of safeguarding democracy and human rights.

a7032.speaker: United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Promotion and Protection of Freedom of Opinion and Expression (UN Human Rights Council, 2017)
a7032.name: United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Promotion and Protection of Freedom of Opinion and Expression (UN Human Rights Council
a7032.speech: Highlighted the dangers of weaponizing speech to erode democratic governance, warning that unchecked hate speech can contribute to polarization, political instability, and even mass atrocities.

a7032.speaker: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum (USHMM, 2014) and the Global Network Against Hate Speech (2020)
a7032.name: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum (USHMM
a7032.title: 2014) and the Global Network Against Hate Speech (2020)
a7032.speech: Documented instances where inflammatory rhetoric has preceded violence, as seen in the Rwandan genocide and ethnic conflicts in the Balkans.

a7032.speaker: International IDEA (2021)
a7032.name: International IDEA (2021)
a7032.speech: The Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) possesses regulatory mechanisms to oversee campaign rhetoric, but enforcement has been inconsistent, largely due to political considerations and institutional weaknesses.

a7032.speaker: Gambia Information and Communications Act (2009)
a7032.name: Gambia Information and Communications Act (2009)
a7032.speech: The country's media regulatory framework lacks explicit provisions on hate speech in digital spaces, thereby allowing unregulated online discourse to flourish.

a7032.speaker: Center for Democracy and Development (CDD) in West Africa (2022 study)
a7032.name: Center for Democracy and Development (CDD) in West Africa (2022 study)
a7032.speech: Highlighted the increasing use of digital platforms to propagate hate speech in the region, often exacerbating ethnic and political tensions.

a7032.speaker: Kenya National Cohesion and Integration Act (2008)
a7032.name: Kenya National Cohesion and Integration Act (2008)
a7032.speech: Criminalizes hate speech and includes provisions allowing for the electoral disqualification of candidates found guilty of inflammatory rhetoric.

a7032.speaker: South Africa Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA, 2000)
a7032.name: South Africa Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA
a7032.speech: Enforces strict provisions against hate speech in political contexts, offering a legal framework that balances free speech with the need to prevent harmful rhetoric.

a7032.speaker: UNESCO (2021)
a7032.name: UNESCO (2021)
a7032.speech: Empirical evidence from countries that have implemented such measures suggests that proactive legal intervention, combined with public awareness campaigns and independent regulatory bodies, can effectively mitigate the spread of divisive rhetoric and enhance social cohesion.

a7032.speaker: International Foundation for Electoral Systems (IFES, 2020)
a7032.name: International Foundation for Electoral Systems (IFES
a7032.speech: Emphasizes that clear legal frameworks are essential in countering hate speech during elections, making such a bill a necessary measure.

a7032.speaker: Council of Europe (2019 toolkit on combating hate speech during elections)
a7032.name: Council of Europe (2019 toolkit on combating hate speech during elections)
a7032.speech: Highlights the importance of equipping electoral management bodies with the authority to enforce such regulations effectively.

a7032.speaker: United Nations (2019)
a7032.name: United Nations (2019)
a7032.speech: Underscores the role of education in fostering inclusive societies and reducing the spread of hate speech, making civic education an essential tool for electoral integrity.

a7032.speaker: German Ministry of Justice (2017) / Germany's Network Enforcement Act (NetzDG)
a7032.name: German Ministry of Justice (2017) / Germany's Network Enforcement Act (NetzDG)
a7032.speech: Requires social media platforms to remove hate speech within 24 hours of reporting.

a7080.speaker: Dr. Jim Yonazi, Permanent Secretary of the Prime Minister's Office (Tanzania)
a7080.name: Dr. Jim Yonazi
a7080.title: Permanent Secretary of the Prime Minister's Office (Tanzania)
a7080.speech: Stated that the initiative is part of the government's broader efforts to address emergencies and disasters that pose threats to human, animal, and environmental health: “In collaboration with sectoral ministries and the USAID-funded Global Health Security project implemented by CIHEB Tanzania, the Prime Minister's Office has initiated this online training to enhance the capacity of service providers in these critical sectors” ; urged leaders and employees from various sectors to actively participate in the sessions, noting that expert facilitators would deliver a wide range of topics designed to boost national preparedness and response to infectious disease outbreaks, crop pests, antimicrobial resistance, and food safety issues.

a7080.speaker: Brigadier General Hosea Ndagala, Director of Disaster Management in the Prime Minister's Office
a7080.name: Brigadier General Hosea Ndagala
a7080.title: Director of Disaster Management in the Prime Minister's Office
a7080.speech: Explained that the training is expected to enhance the effectiveness of professionals in tackling key challenges, including zoonotic diseases, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), biological hazards, food safety, and non-communicable diseases; further noted that the training would involve professionals from a range of sectors, including health, environment, livestock, and fisheries.

a7080.speaker: Suzanne Nchalla, representing the Director of the Department of Health and Nutrition Services in the President's Office – Regional Administration and Local Government (TAMISEMI)
a7080.name: Suzanne Nchalla
a7080.title: representing the Director of the Department of Health and Nutrition Services in the President's Office – Regional Administration and Local Government (TAMISEMI)
a7080.speech: Said the program will help primary-level health workers better understand the One Health concept, thus improving service delivery within communities: “PO-RALG (TAMISEMI) will ensure that primary healthcare workers participate fully in this training. We will mobilize and oversee local government leaders to ensure they attend the scheduled sessions to achieve the intended goals of this initiative.”

a7080.speaker: Dr. Otilia Gowelle, representing the Chief Government Medical Officer
a7080.name: Dr. Otilia Gowelle
a7080.title: representing the Chief Government Medical Officer
a7080.speech: Highlighted the Ministry of Health's recognition of the importance of cross-sectoral and stakeholder collaboration in preparing for and responding to disease outbreaks and other health-related emergencies: “The Ministry of Health is both a participant and a key beneficiary of this initiative. We will continue to promote the participation of a wide range of professionals, including nurses, doctors, pharmacists, health officers, lab specialists, and others working in healthcare facilities” ; reaffirmed the Ministry's commitment to offering continuous support wherever necessary to ensure the successful implementation of the One Health training program.

a7135.speaker: Some public health experts (South Africa)
a7135.name: Some public health experts (South Africa)
a7135.speech: say the Covid-19 vaccine doses destined to be binned next month are 'a shocking indictment' and that questions need to be asked about how effective the country's vaccination drive has been ; said the planned destruction casted a damning spotlight on how South Africa's Covid-19 vaccination campaign had missed the mark.

a7135.speaker: Our World in Data
a7135.name: Our World in Data
a7135.speech: South Africa's fully vaccinated population stood at 33% as of September 2022.

a7135.speaker: Some public health researchers and specialists in South Africa
a7135.name: Some public health researchers and specialists in South Africa
a7135.speech: are pinning the failure to get shots into arms not on people's deepening complacency or vaccine hesitancy but on what they say is the Department of Health's missteps and mistakes in managing the national vaccination drive since vaccines arrived in the country in the first quarter of 2021.

a7135.speaker: Professor Francois Venter, divisional director of Wits University's health platform Ezintsha and former member of the Ministerial Advisory Committee
a7135.name: Professor Francois Venter
a7135.title: divisional director of Wits University's health platform Ezintsha and former member of the Ministerial Advisory Committee
a7135.speech: "That these vaccines are going to be destroyed is a shocking indictment of a vaccination programme that has been badly run from inception. What is incomprehensible is why there was no expertise in mass public health programmes from the beginning." ; "From the start, there was no proper budget for advertising the vaccination services, there was no real strategy around what the key messaging was going to be, and the Department of Health just expected people to arrive at a local facility and get vaccinated." ; Said demand-creation combined creativity, accurate and consistent messaging, and urgency to get widespread buy-in ; added the first misstep was the halt in the rollout of Astra Zeneca vaccines in February 2021 ; said the EVDS (Electronic Verification Data System) failed to have substantial population penetration and now the "wheels have fallen off" of the campaign.

a7135.speaker: SA Coronavirus portal data
a7135.name: SA Coronavirus portal data
a7135.speech: by 11 September, 37 535 745 vaccine doses had been administered.

a7135.speaker: SA Medical Research Council (SAMRC) estimates
a7135.name: SA Medical Research Council (SAMRC) estimates
a7135.speech: estimated the country had seen around 330 000 excess natural deaths since 3 May 2020 - with likely more than 270 000 of those directly due to Covid-19; in 2022 there have been just over 42 000 excess natural deaths.

a7135.speaker: Department of Health of South Africa
a7135.name: Department of Health of South Africa
a7135.speech: insisted the vaccination programme was on track ; said it was trying to extend the October expiry date by three months but was awaiting SA Health Products Regulatory Authority (SAHPRA) approval, and that it had also tried to offload the 8.5 million near-expiry vaccine doses to other countries.

a7135.speaker: Foster Mohale, Department of Health spokesperson
a7135.name: Foster Mohale
a7135.title: Department of Health spokesperson
a7135.speech: "There is no problem with the national vaccination campaign. Vaccines are available, the vaccination programme has been integrated into the primary healthcare delivery system, and communication continues in all national media." ; "The challenge is that the public is complacent that there is no or low perceived risk. This is a complex challenge in a society that is easily influenced by inaccuracies and misinformation spread on social media." ; added the vaccination programme continued with an eye on the possibility of another Covid-19 wave, but admitted they faced competing priorities: "The health system has to care for millions of people with other health conditions and needs and dedicated resources are not possible for Covid-19."

a7135.speaker: Foster Mohale, Department of Health spokesperson
a7135.name: Foster Mohale
a7135.title: Department of Health spokesperson
a7135.speech: Said it had to be factored in that 7.9 million doses of the Pfizer vaccine, out of the 39 million doses received by South Africa, were a donation from the US government ; said the "environmentally approved" disposal would come with its own price tag, adding estimates were "R18 and R25 per kilogram of waste disposed and a tray of 1 170 doses weighs approximately 1.2 kilograms".

a7135.speaker: Foster Mohale, Department of Health spokesperson
a7135.name: Foster Mohale
a7135.title: Department of Health spokesperson
a7135.speech: Said the government had approached the African Union and COVAX facility, and added the challenge was that any recipient country had to agree to the "no-fault compensation scheme", which indemnified manufacturers in the event of any adverse events due to the vaccine.

a7135.speaker: Foster Mohale, Department of Health spokesperson
a7135.name: Foster Mohale
a7135.title: Department of Health spokesperson
a7135.speech: Said the Vaccine Ministerial Advisory Committee had advised against mass vaccination of "small children", though vaccination for immune-compromised children between five and 11 was encouraged, and added the EVDS was being adapted to accommodate this population cohort ; said "further boosters over time to accommodate waning immunity are under evaluation".

a7135.speaker: South African government
a7135.name: South African government
a7135.speech: will not disclose the cost of procuring the vaccines, citing "contractual agreements".

a7135.speaker: Zweli Mkhize, then-health minister
a7135.name: Zweli Mkhize
a7135.title: then-health minister
a7135.speech: told Parliament in April 2021 that both Johnson & Johnson and Pfizer were selling their vaccines to the country at US$10 per dose with no refunds or cancellations permitted.

a7135.speaker: Lynne Wilkinson, public health specialist
a7135.name: Lynne Wilkinson
a7135.title: public health specialist
a7135.speech: Said allowing the vaccines to go to waste without alternative campaigns to make sure they were used was a travesty, especially as vaccination rates in the country were so low and the unknowns around long Covid still posed potential health burdens for sufferers ; "Government needs to think out of the box now by making an additional vaccine accessible and available for whoever wants one or running vaccination blitz days or working with religious leaders to vaccinate at gatherings, for instance." ; said more than a year down the line into vaccination, there should have been lessons learnt to inform a better vaccination strategy going forward ; added the exit of corruption tainted Mkhize should also have been a moment for stronger leadership and revived confidence in vaccination rather than vagueness that had now allowed people to self-assess the Covid risk.

a7135.speaker: Lynne Wilkinson, public health specialist
a7135.name: Lynne Wilkinson
a7135.title: public health specialist
a7135.speech: Said that at the vaccination drive she spearheaded at the Bulungula Incubator in the Eastern Cape village of Nqileni in 2021 they achieved more than 95% vaccination rates for over 60s within weeks, even in a deep rural setting: "We activated all our community resources - meeting elders, going door to door and using community radio and making information clear and available."

a7135.speaker: Professor Kate Alexander, University of Johannesburg's Centre for Social Change
a7135.name: Professor Kate Alexander
a7135.title: University of Johannesburg's Centre for Social Change
a7135.speech: Said low vaccination rates came down to inequality, not vaccine hesitancy, and pointed out it was not a question of money either, with significant overseas donor money having been pumped into the country via the likes of USAID to accelerate the vaccination rollout ; "Government just doesn't have a clue about how to deal with issues of inequality, so hesitancy becomes an argument by which the government blames ordinary people for the vaccine uptake instead of working on simple interventions to get rid of barriers. Government also doesn't know how to relate to community-based organisations and focuses on existing 'leadership' rather than younger activists. Big NGOs have a similar problem." ; added interventions could be better accessed to information about vaccination sites, flexible operating hours for vaccination sites, addressing transport problems to get to sites, and mobilising community groups, like young people, to get the message across.

a7135.speaker: Professor Kate Alexander, University of Johannesburg's Centre for Social Change
a7135.name: Professor Kate Alexander
a7135.title: University of Johannesburg's Centre for Social Change
a7135.speech: Warned failure to change direction would put the remaining 10 million vaccine doses in stockpile in similar jeopardy of expiring before being used up; "It's scandalous and a shambles," she said of the inaction ; joined the growing call for an inquiry into South Africa's handling of the pandemic and vaccination campaign: "An inquiry should be accessible to the public and have the right to subpoena evidence. The low level of vaccination is primarily a question for social science whose practitioners would also have something valuable to say ... if the relevant data was made publicly available."

a7288.speaker: Yusuf Maitama Tuggar, Nigeria's Minister of Foreign Affairs
a7288.name: Yusuf Maitama Tuggar
a7288.title: Nigeria's Minister of Foreign Affairs
a7288.speech: Has called for urgent global reforms to promote economic equity, peace, and security at the ongoing G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Johannesburg.

a7288.speaker: Yusuf Maitama Tuggar, Nigeria's Minister of Foreign Affairs
a7288.name: Yusuf Maitama Tuggar
a7288.title: Nigeria's Minister of Foreign Affairs
a7288.speech: Congratulated South Africa on assuming the G20 Presidency and expressed Nigeria's full support for its priorities, including disaster resilience, debt sustainability, just energy transition, and the harnessing of critical minerals for inclusive growth.

a7288.speaker: Alkasim Abdulkadir, Special Assistant on Media and Communications Strategy to the Minister of Foreign Affairs (statement)
a7288.name: Alkasim Abdulkadir
a7288.title: Special Assistant on Media and Communications Strategy to the Minister of Foreign Affairs (statement)
a7288.speech: A statement by his Special Assistant on Media and Communications Strategy, Alkasim Abdulkadir on Thursday said while addressing global conflicts and humanitarian crises, Tuggar urged the G20 to strengthen mechanisms for peaceful conflict resolution, humanitarian assistance, and African-led peace initiatives.

a7288.speaker: Yusuf Maitama Tuggar, Nigeria's Minister of Foreign Affairs
a7288.name: Yusuf Maitama Tuggar
a7288.title: Nigeria's Minister of Foreign Affairs
a7288.speech: Urged the G20 to strengthen mechanisms for peaceful conflict resolution, humanitarian assistance, and African-led peace initiatives. He also emphasized the need for a comprehensive approach to combating terrorism, focusing on security as well as socio-economic development through investments in education, healthcare, and job creation.

a7288.speaker: Yusuf Maitama Tuggar, Nigeria's Minister of Foreign Affairs
a7288.name: Yusuf Maitama Tuggar
a7288.title: Nigeria's Minister of Foreign Affairs
a7288.speech: Reiterated Nigeria's call for urgent reforms in multilateral institutions, arguing that the current global system does not adequately represent the realities of developing nations. He also highlighted tax justice as a key issue, urging the G20 to support President Bola Ahmed Tinubu's proposals to combat capital flight and tax evasion by multinational corporations.

a7288.speaker: Yusuf Maitama Tuggar, Nigeria's Minister of Foreign Affairs
a7288.name: Yusuf Maitama Tuggar
a7288.title: Nigeria's Minister of Foreign Affairs
a7288.speech: Nigeria raised concerns over illicit financial flows (IFFs), which drain billions from Africa annually through corruption and illegal trade practices. Tuggar called for greater transparency in global financial transactions, stricter regulations on tax havens, and stronger international cooperation to recover stolen assets.

a7288.speaker: Yusuf Maitama Tuggar, Nigeria's Minister of Foreign Affairs
a7288.name: Yusuf Maitama Tuggar
a7288.title: Nigeria's Minister of Foreign Affairs
a7288.speech: He also emphasized that the solidarity, equity, and sustainability must guide the G20's actions, urging global leaders to build a fairer and more inclusive world. Nigeria, he reaffirmed, remains committed to working with international partners to ensure no nation is left behind.

a7362.speaker: Kendrick Lamar, rapper (lyrics)
a7362.name: Kendrick Lamar
a7362.title: rapper (lyrics)
a7362.speech: "I'm not sure why I'm infatuated with death?" ; "Maybe it's because I'm a dreamer and sleep is the cousin of death!"

a7362.speaker: Kendrick Lamar, rapper
a7362.name: Kendrick Lamar
a7362.title: rapper
a7362.speech: Reflected in an interview with Signed Media: "There was smoke everywhere and my dad had a bunch of stolen car rims [he had looted] in the back seat he took from the Compton Swap Meet." ; "My pops and my uncle were both involved in the Watts riots! LA is very sensitive and prideful of its people. We literally burned down our old neighbourhoods because of our anger over Rodney King."

a7362.speaker: 9th Wonder, North Carolina rap producer
a7362.name: 9th Wonder
a7362.title: North Carolina rap producer
a7362.speech: "Kendrick Lamar is more like a documentarian than an MC. Kendrick chooses to rap about everything and everyone across the social strata. People might call it 'woke' or 'deep', but I think of it as straight-up reporting. Some rappers leave out a certain section of people in their lyrics, right? Well, Kendrick tries to rap from everyone's perspective."

a7362.speaker: 9th Wonder, North Carolina rap producer
a7362.name: 9th Wonder
a7362.title: North Carolina rap producer
a7362.speech: On how good kid, m.A.A.d city subverted gangsta rap cliches: "Some rappers do come from good homes with loving moms and dads! Not everyone comes from a hardback struggle, or has to be a bad kid just because they come from a bad place. Kendrick knows the power of telling simple American stories about ordinary people doing their best."

a7362.speaker: Marcus J Moore, music journalist and author of The Butterfly Effect: How Kendrick Lamar Ignited The Soul of Black America
a7362.name: Marcus J Moore
a7362.title: music journalist and author of The Butterfly Effect: How Kendrick Lamar Ignited The Soul of Black America
a7362.speech: "Sadly, there's still a segment of the [American] population that doesn't consider rap a viable genre in music, despite its popularity. Such thinking suggests racism and classism, but with Kendrick Lamar, he's the type of rapper who can make fans out of anyone. He's a rapper's rapper with a pop sensibility on stage. And while he's tremendous on his own, he's also had the benefit of guesting with bigger stars like Beyonce and Taylor Swift. I think Kendrick has done a great job over the years of making himself undeniable."

a7362.speaker: Marcus J Moore, music journalist and author
a7362.name: Marcus J Moore
a7362.title: music journalist and author
a7362.speech: "Artists of Kendrick's stature don't usually rock the boat [and change their sound too radically] once they become famous. But he's done so with many of his releases, no matter how popular the previous albums were. He's encouraged others to take creative risks for their music. I think, more than anything, this courage has helped change popular music."

a7362.speaker: Marcus J Moore, music journalist and author
a7362.name: Marcus J Moore
a7362.title: music journalist and author
a7362.speech: Predicts of the Super Bowl performance: "I would prepare for anything! If there's any message that could emanate from Kendrick's Super Bowl performance in New Orleans, I think it could be about the wildfires in Los Angeles and the city's resilience."

a7362.speaker: Marcus J Moore, music journalist and author
a7362.name: Marcus J Moore
a7362.title: music journalist and author
a7362.speech: "Sure, some of his core fans might see his Super Bowl performance as a sell-out move, but I would encourage those listeners to go back and revisit his 2022 album, Mr Morale & The Big Steppers, where he shot back against the notion of being a paragon of virtue." ; "Though listeners may want him to be the same artist and person he was on albums like good kid, m.A.A.d. city and To Pimp a Butterfly, they have to realise that was a decade ago, and if they want that guy, they have to play those albums."

a7362.speaker: Seb Joseph, marketing expert and editor at Digiday
a7362.name: Seb Joseph
a7362.title: marketing expert and editor at Digiday
a7362.speech: Believes the NFL's decision to have Lamar as a half-time performer is supposed to reflect the changing values of their brand and business itself, and says his selection "isn't a risk - it's a statement" ; "If previous Super Bowl performers like Prince, Beyonce and Madonna embodied pop ubiquity, Kendrick represents something just as powerful: cultural gravity. His music isn't always designed for casual singalongs but rather it's built for reflection, resistance and resonance. And in a moment when the NFL is still navigating its own complicated relationship with race, protest and black artistic expression, Kendrick isn't just an artist - they're inviting a movement to the main stage."

a7362.speaker: Seb Joseph, marketing expert and editor at Digiday
a7362.name: Seb Joseph
a7362.title: marketing expert and editor at Digiday
a7362.speech: On whether performing Not Like Us is a risk to advertisers: "The song has transcended the beef. It's fun, it's infectious and it's already been embraced far beyond the hip-hop world. Instead of just a diss track, it's a cultural jolt - one that taps into regional pride, black joy and the communal energy that makes music feel alive. Brands love to co-opt hip-hop culture when it's convenient. They'll put rap lyrics on ad campaigns or with tweets; partner with artists for limited-edition sneakers' and drop hip-hop-inspired Super Bowl commercials - all while keeping a safe distance from the actual violent tensions that shape the genre."

a7362.speaker: Seb Joseph, marketing expert and editor at Digiday
a7362.name: Seb Joseph
a7362.title: marketing expert and editor at Digiday
a7362.speech: "The Super Bowl half-time show isn't just a performance - it's the single biggest branding opportunity in music. It's a 12-minute global ad for an artist's catalogue, cultural impact, and marketability, all broadcast to an audience of over 100 million people." ; "And here's the kicker: performers don't get paid! Instead, the exposure itself becomes the currency, often translating into massive streaming hikes, album sales and brand deals. Take Rihanna in 2023: her streams rose 640% after her performance, and Fenty Beauty reportedly pulled in more than $5 million in media impact value from that subtle but game-changing mid-show makeup touch up. But with the rewards come massive risks." ; "The Super Bowl is a high-stakes, zero-margin-for-error stage where the scrutiny is relentless, the expectations sky-high. If an artist miscalculates, whether it's the energy, the production or the cultural moment they're stepping into, the fallout can be brutal."

a7362.speaker: Seb Joseph, marketing expert and editor at Digiday
a7362.name: Seb Joseph
a7362.title: marketing expert and editor at Digiday
a7362.speech: Hopes to see Lamar perform Alright, believing the protest song's simple message of perseverance is needed now more than ever before: "At a time when history feels like it is repeating itself, when the same battles for justice and dignity are being fought yet again, Kendrick standing on that stage, leading millions in the chorus of 'We gon' be alright,' would be a powerful message. It would say: 'we're still here... and we're not going anywhere.'"

a7362.speaker: Paul A Thompson, Pitchfork
a7362.name: Paul A Thompson
a7362.title: Pitchfork
a7362.speech: Crowning Not Like Us the best song of 2024, wrote: "In the third verse, Kendrick casts Drake as a parasite who leeches off of younger, more inventive rappers in a quest for pyrrhic streaming statements. But by that point he's already turned the biggest pop star on the planet into a punchline."

a7362.speaker: Drake, rapper
a7362.name: Drake
a7362.title: rapper
a7362.speech: Denies Lamar's insinuation that he had relationships with underage women, and has taken legal action against record label Universal Music over the track Not Like Us.
